description:
FCC Recycling Florida, LLC (FCC; previously GEL Corporation) is the onsite recycling services provider at the Volusia County landfill. Volusia County has an agreement for services with FCC and makes this agreement available for any municipality within the county to use. The City utilizes this agreement to provide a local service center for recyclable goods collected in the city.
On October 28, 2014, the City executed an Amended and Restated Agreement with GEL Corporation under the County of Volusia’s contract to provide recyclable materials processing and marketing services.
Amendment No. 1 was executed and approved on December 18, 2018, and Amendment No. 2 was executed and approved on March 7, 2023. Both amendments were processed to maintain consistency with the County of Volusia’s agreement. The current agreement term continues through June 30, 2030.
On July 23, 2026, the County of Volusia executed and approved Amendment No. 3 to its Amended and Restated Agreement with GEL, LLC.
Amendment No. 3 updates the agreement to reflect that GEL, LLC was acquired by FCC Environmental Services, LLC. As part of a corporate restructuring, GEL, LLC assigned its contracts and obligations to FCC Recycling Florida, LLC.
The amendment also updates the recycling processing requirements to a single-stream method (all recyclable items are placed into a single bin without pre-sorting for collection) consistent with the facility’s equipment and operations. The amendment provides for a single stream market value payment as a credit to the processing fee. The City pays a set rate for each ton of co-mingled recycling materials brought to FCC and then receives a credit from FCC based on the market value of what is processed.
title: Approval of Amendment No. 3 to the Amended and Restated Agreement with FCC Recycling Florida, LLC to provide Recyclable Materials Processing and Marketing Services (CA000674)

attachments.name: Amendment No. 1 and Renewal No. 1 Waste Pro

description:
On March 2, 2021, the City entered into a Standard Contract for Services with Waste Pro of Florida, Inc. (Waste Pro), pursuant to RFP #21-01 for Solid Waste Collection & Disposal Services. The initial term of the contract was for five (5) years, from November 1, 2021, continuing to October 31, 2026. The contract provides for a one (1) five (5) year renewal option. This proposed renewal is for the period of November 1, 2026, continuing to October 31, 2031.
Under the proposed amended and renewed contract, Waste Pro will continue its current collection services: residential garbage two times per week, recycling once a week, vegetation and bulk pickup once a week, and commercial container services.
With this renewal, Waste Pro is requesting some modifications to the terms of the contract. The proposed modifications to the general contract terms are summarized below:
Change the requirement from having recycling bins available for customer pickup at Public Works to being delivered by Waste Pro to residents' homes upon request. This system is more convenient for the residents and lessens the need for a Waste Pro representative at the Public Works site.
Waste Pro will continue to provide a dedicated Customer Service Representative (CSR) and a dedicated phone line to service the City. The proposed change allows the employee to be based in Waste Pro's offices. Having a CSR on site in Public Works was not found to be a notable benefit, as almost all contact with customers is by phone and email, and it frees up space in the City's facility.
Change the annual replacement of commercial containers from every year to every three (3) years, as containers are very durable, and it is not necessary to replace them annually (City retains the right to request replacements as needed).
Waste Pro is also requesting rate increases. By contract and based on the original contract bid terms, these rate increases are only allowed one year at a time and cannot be consolidated into one multi-year rate increase. The contract allows for annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) rate increases based on the US Department of Labor, Bureau of Statistics published information, if requested by Waste Pro. CPI rate increases were requested and added to the City's cost in FY24, FY25 and FY26.
The contract also allows for rate increases based on "unusual changes or costs" defined as unusual and unanticipated increases in the cost of doing business. Waste Pro did not receive any rate increases based on unusual changes or costs in the initial 5-year term.
With this proposed amendment, Waste Pro is requesting a one-year rate adjustment for CPI and also adjustments for unusual changes or costs. The justification for unusual changes or costs includes increases in labor rates, fuel, vehicles, vehicle maintenance, insurance, and operational supplies since the beginning of the contract term. The requested rate increases are:
Rate AdjustmentsCurrentFY26/27Residential Pickup$11.17$16.48Residential Recycling$2.79$4.12Commercial Hand Pickup$34.89$34.89Commercial Container$5.80$7.79
The proposed rate changes in this renewal will not create the need for the City to pass on the rate increase to residents and businesses this year. The current rate charged by the City is sufficient to cover the Waste Pro increase to the City in the current Fiscal Year. However, customer rate increases may be needed in future years.
The rate the City charges customers is based on the Waste Pro charge, tipping fees for use of the County landfill, costs of City staffing, and costs for the use of and impacts to City infrastructure.
Even with the proposed increase, solid waste collection in Port Orange remains a good value. The garbage rates Waste Pro charges the City and the City's subsequent end-user rate to the customers have been and would continue to be among the lowest in Volusia County for equivalent service levels.
title: Approval of the Amendment and Renewal of the Standard Contract for Services (CA7306) with Waste Pro of Florida, Inc. for Residential and Commercial City Solid Waste Services

attachments.name: VO-PO-23-142 Day Dock at Riverwalk Park Ph I 1-year Extension AGR w City signature blk
VO-PO-23-142 Day Dock at Riverwalk Park Phase 1 Agr executed

description:
Staff requests approval of an amendment to the project agreement between the City and the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) for the Day Dock at Riverwalk Park Phase I project. Phase I includes completing the design plans for the Day Dock and obtaining all necessary permits from applicable outside review agencies. Phase 1 was completed in September 2025, and project closeout, including the reimbursement request, was sent to FIND in November 2025 within the timeframe established by FIND. Pursuant to the agreement and FIND program rules, the reimbursement request for Phase I funding will be held in accounts payable pending receipt of a construction contract to build the Day Dock (Phase II). FIND can hold this payment for up to one additional year after the project expires.
Staff worked with FIND on this amendment to extend the Phase I completion deadline to September 30, 2026. The amendment would also allow FIND to hold the $92,000 Phase I reimbursement through September 30, 2027, giving the City additional time to finalize the construction contract for the Day Dock. Staff is currently preparing the project for bidding and anticipates awarding the construction contract in early 2027. Construction of the Day Dock (Phase II) is expected to begin in spring 2027, with the goal of completing the project by the end of 2027.
Under the current agreement between the City and FIND, FIND will reimburse the City up to $92,000 for eligible Phase I costs, which total approximately $184,000. Once the City awards the construction contract in early 2027, it will request the $92,000 reimbursement from FIND for Phase I. Extending the reimbursement deadline will ensure the City has sufficient time to complete the contract process and request the reimbursement while moving forward with construction of the Day Dock.
The estimated construction cost for the Day Dock project is $1,620,520. In fall 2025, FIND awarded the City $405,130, representing 25% of the estimated construction cost. Staff subsequently worked with FIND to submit a second application in March 2026. FIND recently notified staff that the City will receive an additional $292,922 in funding for construction of the Day Dock as a result of the second grant application.
Acceptance of the additional $292,922 in funding will be on an upcoming City Council agenda. Once accepted, the City will have a total of $698,052 in FIND funding toward construction of the Day Dock (Phase II), representing approximately 43% of the estimated construction cost.
The project includes a floating dock oriented perpendicular to the shoreline, providing mooring for up to ten (10) vessels up to 35 feet in length, with the potential for future expansion as demand increases. The dock is also designed to accommodate a future water taxi stop. The project includes dredging to establish a navigational access channel connecting the day dock to the adjacent deep-water channel leading to the Intracoastal Waterway (ICW), as well as installing channel markers from the dock to the existing marked channel.
title: Approval of FIND VO-PO-23-142 Day Dock at Riverwalk Park Phase I, Project Agreement Amendment for a 1-Year Extension

description:

The County-owned property in this area is part of the Long Leaf Preserve, making coordination between the City and County particularly important in addressing the properties as a cohesive area.
At Volusia County's November 18, 2025, council meeting, the County awarded seven (7) contracts to provide professional land management services based upon statements of qualifications submitted in response to Request for Statement of Qualifications 25-SQ-146LL Professional Land Management Services, establishing a three-year contract, with the option for two additional one-year extensions. The County Contracts authorize services through task assignments (COPO Task Authorizations). Individual task authorizations issued under the established master contracts will establish the specific scope of services, schedule, and compensation for each project, subject to an appropriated budget and approval by the City Manager, as requested hereinbelow.
Utilizing the existing County Contracts would allow the City to establish contracts with qualified firms to provide needed services related to the City Forest lands. This approach would also facilitate coordination with Volusia County regarding the County-owned portion of the Long Leaf Preserve and the City and County's jointly owned property. Services obtained through these contracts would include the following: Administration of Timber Sales, Reforestation, Wildlife Management, Non-Native and Invasive Species Management, Management Plan Development, Fireline Maintenance & Vegetation Mitigation.
Staff is therefore requesting authorization to use of the above-referenced Volusia County Contracts for services needed for the City-owned and City and County jointly owned properties located off Shunz Road, in accordance with the terms and conditions of said contracts. In addition, staff is requesting City Council authorize the City Manager to review and approve said contracts and any associated task authorizations issued thereunder.

attachments.name: CPH Consulting, LLC - Task Authorization No 5

description:
The City established one of the first permitted Gopher Tortoise Long-Term Recipient Sites in the State of Florida. As a requirement of the permit, annual reporting and maintenance activities need to be conducted. CPH, Inc. has been handling these services for the City for several years through its continuing services contract for Professional Engineering Services (RFSQ #23-18). This Task Authorization is executed annually to continue the required annual monitoring and related field work for compliance with the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation (FWC) Commission permit.
The Gopher Tortoise Long-Term Recipient Sites are located west of the reclaimed reservoirs in the City wellfield. Currently, the Gopher Tortoise Recipient bank has numerous reservation commitments for some 30 projects within the service area, i.e., Florida Department of Transportation, Florida Power & Light, and the Woodhaven development along South Williamson Boulevard.
Amy Daly, CPH Principle Environmental Scientist, is the Authorized Gopher Tortoise Agent named on the City Permit and performs work of a specified nature. The Permit, issued by the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, authorizes the City, through the designated Gopher Tortoise Agent, to conduct the specified activities in association with the relocation of gopher tortoises, subject to applicable rules and provisions set forth in the FWC Permit #GTLR-09-0009C. CPH has successfully completed all annual inspections with FWC agents and submitted all previous, approved triennial reports. The site has received over 1,100 gopher tortoises for protection from development sites within the permitted service area. The City has received net revenue in excess of $500,000 working with CPH, Inc., a statewide firm, and the Authorized Gopher Tortoise Agent on the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission Permit.
CPH has submitted a proposal for $81,570.00 to provide the services required by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission for the Gopher Tortoise Long-Term Recipient Site. These services include the following for all active phases: annual reporting to the Florida Fish & Wildlife Commission, removal and disposal of silt fence, installation of new silt fence, required mortality report, multiple site inspections and meetings with the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission.

description:
This ordinance is an amendment to the Port Orange Police Pension Fund (“Pension Fund”) to implement the pension enhancement set forth in the recently adopted Collective Bargaining Agreements with PBA and IUPA.
The changes are as follows:
The maximum total benefit amount provided under Section 54-130 shall not exceed $125,000.00 (an increase from $95,000) inclusive of any cost of living adjustments to which the member may be entitled.
The revised supplemental benefit (commonly referred to as the medical stipend) will start at $500/month for ten years of service. For each year of service completed over 10, the participant will earn an additional $50/month. This will continue until the participant completes 20 years of service, reaching a maximum monthly supplement benefit of $1,000/month. The current supplemental benefit is $200/month at 10 years of service, with an additional $20/month earned for each year beyond 10 years, up to a $600/month cap.
Tier 1 employee contribution increases to 9% (previously 7.5%). Tier 2 remains 8.0%.
Staff received and reviewed the actuarial impact statement related to this change to the Pension Fund.

attachments.name: Purchase and Sale Contract 1201 Reed Canal

description:
At the March 19, 2024 meeting, the City Council approved Resolution No. 24-04, establishing the City-owned property (Lot 16 - 1201 Reed Canal Road) generally located on the south side of Reed Canal Road, east of Atlantic High School, as surplus and authorizing Staff to market the property for sale. In June 2024, the City’s broker, Colliers International Florida, LLC (Colliers), began marketing the approximately 8.7-acre property for sale.
Location map of the City-owned property (Lot 16) at 1201 Reed Canal Road
In December 2024, the City entered into a contract to sell the property for development as an outdoor storage facility for heavy equipment and construction materials, as well as office and warehouse space. During the purchaser’s due diligence and evaluation of the property, the prospective purchaser determined that the anticipated site-development costs, including the purchase and transportation of fill dirt, were higher than initially expected. As a result, the purchaser subsequently withdrew from the contract, and the proposed sale did not proceed.
Since the withdrawal of the December 2024 contract, the City has received a limited number of inquiries regarding the property. However, no additional purchase contracts were submitted until the latest contract was received in mid-August 2026 from Daytona RV, Inc.
Daytona RV, Inc. has proposed to purchase 1201 Reed Canal Road for $625,000, with the intent to develop the property as an age-restricted (55-plus) manufactured home community. Under the proposed contract, closing on the property would be contingent upon approval of a Future Land Use (FLU) amendment and an amendment to the Master Development Agreement (MDA) for the Crystal Lake Planned Unit Development (PUD).
A manufactured home park is not an allowed use under the current FLU designation and MDA for the Crystal Lake PUD. To facilitate the proposed development, Daytona RV Inc. would submit applications requesting an amendment to the FLU designation for the property from Warehouse/Industrial to Urban Medium-Density Residential (4–8 units per acre) and an amendment to the MDA to allow a manufactured home park.
The proposed FLU designation would generally be consistent with the existing FLU designations of the properties immediately adjacent to the subject property, including Lamplighter Mobile Home Park to the south and The Mira multifamily development to the north. The subject property also abuts Atlantic High School, designated Government/Public Use, to the east, and a warehouse/office complex, designated Warehouse/Industrial, to the west.
Location map of the City-owned property (Lot 16) at 1201 Reed Canal Road, showing the Future Land Use (FLU) designations of the surrounding properties and the proposed FLU designation for Lot 16.
The FLU and MDA amendment applications will be processed and considered in accordance with the City’s applicable review and approval procedures, including review by the Planning Commission and consideration by the City Council. Approval of the purchase contract would not, by itself, constitute approval of the proposed FLU or MDA amendments. If the required amendments are approved and all other applicable conditions of the purchase contract are satisfied, Daytona RV, Inc. anticipates closing on the property in spring 2027.

description:
Task Authorization No. 1 with Ohlson Lavoie Corporation is for design and construction phase services for a prefabricated restroom building at the City Center Sports Complex which will serve Fields 4 and 5 and the soccer field. This task was initiated in February 2024. However, shortly thereafter, field depressions were identified on the soccer field and Field 3. Due to the proximity of these depressions to the proposed restroom site and uncertainty regarding the extent and timing of the necessary field repairs, the project was placed on hold effective May 1, 2024. At that time, design services were complete, and the project was ready for construction. This amendment extends the contract term only and allows the architect to complete construction-phase services and project closeout.
The scope and extent of the field repair work have since been determined, and it has been confirmed that the repairs will not interfere with the restroom project. As a result, the project resumed and construction began in July 2026. Because the project remained on hold for approximately two years, the original contract term under Task Authorization No. 1 has expired.
Amendment No. 1 extends the contract term only and does not modify the scope of services or increase costs. description:
This agenda item is for the City Council to ratify the retention of the law firms of Baron & Budd, P.C., Simonsen Sussman LLP, Tessitore Mari Scott, PLLC, and Halling & Cayo, S.C. to represent the City of Port Orange in a lawsuit filed against manufacturers of fire trucks and fire apparatus and related defendants for damages incurred by the City as a result of unfair and anti-competitive business practices in violation of the antitrust laws.
Fire Chief Wulfing first notified the City Attorney’s Office of a potential class action related to the purchases of fire apparatus. Chief Wulfing noticed that the prices for fire apparatus have steeply inclined over recent years while the wait times regularly exceed one year and recently closer to three years for a custom fire truck build. Our review of the potential action revealed that over the past decade, a series of mergers and acquisitions has consolidated the fire apparatus industry among a small number of manufacturers. Governmental entities across the country — more than 40 to date, ranging from large metropolitan fire agencies to smaller cities and fire districts — have filed individual lawsuits alleging that this consolidation reduced competition and caused substantial increases in fire apparatus prices, restricted supply, significantly longer delivery times, and restrictive practices involving replacement parts and warranties.
The claims are asserted principally under the federal antitrust laws, including Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and Section 7 of the Clayton Act, together with related state-law claims; federal antitrust law provides for trebling of proven damages, together with injunctive relief and recovery of attorney fees and costs. The cases have been consolidated for coordinated pretrial proceedings as multidistrict litigation in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, In re: Fire Apparatus Antitrust Litigation, MDL No. 3179.
Baron & Budd, P.C. and Simonsen Sussman LLP serve as Court-appointed co-lead counsel for the non-class governmental plaintiffs in the litigation and would handle the national antitrust, economic, expert, and discovery work, while Tessitore Mari Scott, PLLC would serve as Florida local counsel and maintain direct contact with the City. Potential damages the City may assert include the overcharges and other economic harm resulting from its fire apparatus purchases. The firms would represent the City on a contingency fee basis at 25% of any net recovery, with all litigation costs and expenses advanced by counsel and reimbursed only from a recovery; if there is no recovery, the City would owe no attorney fees and would have no obligation to reimburse the advanced costs. The City would pursue its own individual claim and would retain ultimate authority over its case, including the authority to approve or reject any settlement. Pursuing an individual claim now would not preclude the City from participating in any class that may later be certified.
Dale A. Scott is a Partner with Tessitore Mari Scott, PLLC, located in Lake Mary, Florida, and would serve as the City's Florida local counsel; Baron & Budd, P.C. is a national litigation firm experienced in complex and multidistrict litigation, and Simonsen Sussman LLP is an antitrust-focused firm. The litigation overview and the proposed professional services agreement are attached hereto for your consideration.
In the interests of preserving the City's claim related to a 2022 purchase of fire apparatus that was approaching the statute of limitations cut-off, the City Attorney engaged special counsel and authorized the complaint be filed on behalf of the City subject to review and ratification by the City Council.

PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (August 27, 2026): Recommended ​Approval ​4-0
The subject property is located at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard, at the northwest corner of Clyde Morris Boulevard and Dunlawton Avenue, and is part of the Robinson Planned Commercial Development (PCD), which was approved by the Port Orange City Council in 1987. The Robinson PCD established the permitted uses and building dimensional requirements applicable to the development of the subject property. The subject property was developed as a bank in 1989 and operated as a bank for approximately 37 years. The site has been vacant for approximately five years.
Location map of 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard
According to the property owner/applicant, the requested changes to the Master Development Agreement (MDA) for the Robinson PCD would allow the existing bank drive-thru canopy to be enclosed and converted into additional office space, which would be incorporated into the existing building. If approved, the vacant bank building would be redeveloped as a dental office for White Wolf Dental. The proposed redevelopment of the building and site would include interior and exterior renovations to the existing building, enclosure of the existing drive-thru canopy, and installation of new landscaping throughout the site.
The property owner/applicant requests the following amendments to the MDA for the Robinson PCD based on the redevelopment plan for the building and site:To reduce the internal side yard setback from 15 feet to 10 feet. The requested 10-foot side yard building setback is consistent with the current standard side yard building setback requirements in the Land Development Code (LDC) for comparable City zoning districts that allow office and institutional uses, such as Professional Office, Neighborhood Commercial, Office/Residential Transition, and Government/Public Use. The requested 10-foot side-yard building setback is consistent with current side-yard building setback requirements in other non-residential zoning districts that support office uses.
To remove the 75-foot building separation requirement and allow the building separation to be as required by the Florida Building Code (FBC) and National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). Current City dimensional standards for commercial and office zoning districts in Chapter 17 of the LDC do not establish a specific building separation requirement; instead, building separation is determined based on required setbacks and compliance with the FBC and NFPA standards. Consistent with the City's current development review process, building separation is evaluated based on compliance with applicable FBC and NFPA requirements rather than on a city-established building separation standard. The proposed amendment would remove the building separation requirement from the MDA and allow the lot to be redeveloped in a manner consistent with the applicable FBC and NFPA requirements, as well as the side setbacks established for the subject and adjacent properties. If the MDA amendment is approved, the side yard building setback for the property at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard would be reduced to 10 feet. The adjacent property to the south has a required minimum side-yard building setback of 15 feet, with an actual setback of approximately 26 feet. Therefore, the separation between the building on the adjacent property to the south of the subject property and the enclosed bank canopy would be 36 feet, which exceeds the applicable building separation requirements under the FBC and NFPA standards, which require a separation of greater than 10 feet.
Picture of the existing building at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard shows the canopy area to be enclosed and the adjacent office to the south, with the proposed building separation labeled.
The staff report is attached for more detail.

description:
Currently, the Code of Ordinances provides a three-day limit for setup and take-down before and after a Special Event. The Code also provides a process for City Council to approve an extended timeframe when setup and take-down activities exceed the three-day limitation.
The Code of Ordinances states that Special Events associated with a legal holiday or seasonal event, such as spring landscaping, Christmas tree sales, Halloween pumpkin sales, or sparkler sales, shall not exceed forty (40) consecutive calendar days and are limited to three (3) days prior to the event for setup and three (3) days after the event for take-down.
In recent years, some seasonal events have required additional setup and take-down time due to operational requirements. For example, last year, Home Depot and Lowe’s were approved for an additional 30 days of setup/take-down time outside the actual event timeframe [e.g. Special Event ran from November 15, 2025, through December 24, 2025 (39 days); the tent and sales area set-up begin on October 24, 2025, and was completed November 14, 2025 (21 days); take-down was completed on January 2, 2026 (9 days)]. These requirements may include tent and electrical installation and inspection, the setup of seasonal merchandise (Christmas trees, pumpkins, etc.), internal business or tenant procedures for preparing and closing the site for sales, and scheduling the removal of tents or other rented structures.
After several years of requests for extended setup and take-down periods being brought before and approved by City Council for seasonal events, Staff is proposing an amendment to Chapter 58, Article III, Special Events, Section 58-53.
The proposed amendment would allow additional setup and take-down time beyond the three-day limitation for seasonal events involving the sale of seasonal merchandise, such as Christmas trees and pumpkins, to be approved by the Administrative Official. Approval would be based on a determination that the additional time requested is justified by the operational circumstances of the event. This may include the time reasonably necessary for the delivery, placement, setup, or removal of equipment, tents, inventory, displays, or similar materials.
The proposed amendment would also include language requiring tents, other temporary structures, and merchandise associated with the event to be secured or removed in the event of an approaching hurricane, tropical storm, or other significant weather event.
If the Administrative Official does not approve the requested additional time for setup and takedown before and after a Special Event, the applicant may still request approval from the City Council.

description:
Staff will provide a brief overview of the data center industry, the varying scale of these facilities, current State requirements, the City's existing regulatory framework, and potential approaches for addressing data centers through the City's planning and development regulations.
State Requirements: In 2026, the State of Florida enacted legislation addressing data centers and other large-load electric customers. Florida law defines a “large-scale data center” as a data center at a single location with an anticipated monthly peak electric load of 50 megawatts (MW) or more, based on the highest average load over a 15-minute interval. For comparison, if a 50-MW load was sustained continuously, 24 hours a day, for a full year, it would represent about 438 million kilowatt-hours of electricity, roughly equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about 40,000 U.S. homes. Large-scale data centers can vary widely in size based on design, power requirements, and cooling systems. As a general reference, large facilities may include a single building or multiple buildings totaling more than 100,000 square feet, with sites potentially ranging from 100 to 300 acres. The site may also include electrical and utility infrastructure, cooling equipment, stormwater facilities, buffers, and areas for future expansion.
The legislation adds requirements for large-scale data centers and large-load customers while allowing local governments to retain authority over comprehensive planning and land development regulations. The legislation does not require local governments to permit data centers in all zoning districts or preempt a local government's ability to regulate the location and development of such facilities through its Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code (LDC).
The new State requirements also address water and electric utility considerations associated with large-scale data centers and large-load customers. Water-resource permitting for large-scale data centers must be consistent with applicable local zoning regulations, comprehensive plans, and consumptive use permits. The legislation also requires large-load customers to ensure the costs of serving them are appropriately assigned and not shifted to general utility ratepayers. Data centers or large-load customers below the 50-MW threshold are not subject to the new requirements that apply to large-scale data centers or large-load customers but remain subject to other applicable State and local regulations.
City's Existing Regulatory Framework: Under the City's current LDC, data centers of any size are not specifically addressed, nor do they appear to fall within an existing use classification that would allow them to be treated as a similar use. The LDC provides that any use not specifically permitted is prohibited. Therefore, data centers are not currently an allowed use in the City. Leaving data centers undefined or unmentioned creates uncertainty about whether they fit within an existing use category and whether the comprehensive plan authorizes the use. It also forces the City to resolve broader policy questions during individual quasi-judicial proceedings.
The LDC provides a process for considering uses that are not specifically identified in the Code. Unlisted uses may be considered through the Conditional Use process to determine whether they are appropriate for the proposed location and compatible with surrounding development. Conditional Uses require City Council approval.
For a proposed data center, this process would allow the City to evaluate the specific characteristics and location of the facility. Depending on the proposal, the review could address setbacks and separation from residential uses, noise, building scale, water resources, electrical infrastructure, landscaping and buffering, backup generators, traffic, emergency services, compatibility with surrounding development, and other potential impacts.
Potential Next Steps: Following the presentation, City Council may provide direction regarding how the City should proceed. The following options are presented for Council consideration and are not staff recommendations:
1. Consider a Temporary Moratorium: Direct staff to evaluate or prepare a temporary moratorium on the acceptance or processing of applications for data centers while the City studies potential Comprehensive Plan and LDC amendments. A temporary moratorium could give staff additional time to research the City's regulatory options and develop potential regulations for Council consideration. Resolution No. 26-51 has been prepared to provide the required notification of the City's intent to adopt a 12-month moratorium on issuing development orders, building permits, zoning verification letters, special exception and conditional use approvals, and change-of-use applications for any-sized data center on private property within the City of Port Orange. The proposed moratorium would apply to all data center types, including large-scale data centers, other large-load utility users, and smaller facilities that meet the technical definition of a data center.
If the resolution is approved, staff will prepare an ordinance establishing a twelve (12) month moratorium, which will be presented to the City Council for approval in November. During the moratorium, staff will evaluate the potential impacts of data centers of all sizes and other large-load utility users and develop potential regulatory approaches as described below in bullet #2. Any proposed Comprehensive Plan or Land Development Code amendments will follow the standard city public-hearing processes for these types of amendments.
2. Develop Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code Amendments: Direct staff to prepare potential Comprehensive Plan and LDC amendments establishing specific policies and regulations for data centers. Potential regulations could address definitions, appropriate zoning districts, whether data centers should be permitted or subject to Conditional Use review, and development standards addressing issues such as setbacks, separation from residential uses, noise, building scale, water resources, electrical infrastructure, landscaping and buffering, backup generators, traffic, emergency services, and other potential impacts. However, without a moratorium in place while the regulations are being developed, the City would have to resolve applications through the conditional use review process.
3. Maintain the Existing Regulatory Framework: Take no action at this time and continue to evaluate any proposed data center under the City's existing Comprehensive Plan and LDC, including the City's Conditional Use process for unlisted use. Case-by-case review without data center-specific criteria presents greater risks of inconsistent decisions, inefficient proceedings, and challenges alleging arbitrary treatment or unbridled discretion.
4. Provide Other Direction to Staff: Provide additional direction regarding specific issues or regulatory approaches that City Council would like staff to evaluate as part of the City's continued review of data centers.
title: Data Center Presentation and Resolution No. 26-51 - Intent to Adopt a Moratorium for Any-Sized Data Center on Private Property

description:
Engineering Staff requests City Council approval to award ITB #26-04, Reclaimed Water Reservoir Improvements, to J.D. Weber Construction Company in the amount of $2,350,772.87, and authorize contingency for unforeseen conditions in an amount not to exceed $100,000.
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) operating permit for the Water Reclamation Facility limits the amount of discharge allowed to the adjacent wetland from the reclaimed water reservoir system. In late 2021, the City exceeded the permitted discharge limit. This led to FDEP issuing a consent order requiring the City to address this matter. The City retained Mead & Hunt to evaluate the effluent disposal system to identify the cause of the excessive discharge and develop a solution. Several alternatives were considered, including construction of a new reservoir and expansion of existing storage facilities. After evaluating the options, the City selected the most cost-effective solution: increasing the storage capacity of the existing reclaimed water reservoirs by raising the reservoir berms and overflow elevations. These improvements will provide additional wet-weather storage and reduce the likelihood of exceeding the permitted discharge limit in the future.During the preliminary design process, City Operations Staff identified a recurring maintenance issue associated with the existing pipe connection between Reservoir A and Reservoir B. The pipe frequently becomes obstructed by debris associated with alligator nesting activity, preventing water from flowing between the reservoirs as intended. When the connection becomes blocked, water levels in Reservoir B approach the overflow elevation, reducing operational flexibility and requiring Staff intervention to restore normal operations.To improve system reliability and operational efficiency, the project scope was expanded to include removal of the existing interconnecting pipe and construction of an open-channel connector between the reservoirs.
Project DescriptionThe project will enhance the City's reclaimed water storage and distribution system through several improvements, including:
Construction of an open-channel connection between Reservoir A and Reservoir B to replace the existing interconnecting pipe.
Raising the Reservoir B berm approximately one foot to increase reclaimed water storage capacity by approximately 15 million gallons.
Improvements to reclaimed water pump station yard piping.
Upgrades to electrical systems and controls to improve operational flexibility and reliability.
Upon completion, the project will increase reclaimed water storage capacity, improve system performance, enhance operational reliability, and satisfy the corrective actions necessary to address FDEP requirements.
On June 24, 2026, six sealed bids were received. J.D. Weber Construction Company was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder. The project is included in the approved Capital Improvement Program (CIP) budget. Following is a breakdown of the six bids received.

description:
Dredging & Marine Consultants, LLC (DMC) completed the design and permitting for the Day Dock at Riverwalk Park project in Fall 2025 pursuant to Task Authorization No. 5, which was approved by City Council in Fall 2023. The term of Task Authorization No. 5 continues until the completed project has been accepted by the City.
To facilitate putting the project out to bid this fall, with construction anticipated to begin in early 2027, additional services are being requested under Amendment No. 1 to Task Authorization No. 5 for bidding assistance, construction management, inspection, and support to the City with Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) grant reporting. DMC will perform these additional services for a lump sum fee of $56,430.00. Funds for the additional services are budgeted in the Day Dock at Riverwalk Park project.
The design plans for the Day Dock have been completed, and all necessary permits have been obtained. The project includes a floating dock oriented perpendicular to the shoreline, providing mooring for up to ten (10) vessels up to 35 feet in length, with the potential for future expansion as demand increases. The dock is also designed to accommodate a future water taxi stop. The project includes a dredging profile to establish a navigational access channel connecting the day dock to the adjacent deep-water channel leading to the Intracoastal Waterway (ICW), as well as the installation of channel markers from the dock to the existing marked channel.
The estimated construction cost for the Riverwalk Park Day Dock project is $1,620,520. The City initially requested $810,260, or 50% of the estimated construction cost, in funding from FIND. In Fall 2025, FIND awarded the City $405,130, representing 25% of the total construction cost, due to limited funding availability and the high number of qualified projects submitted.
Staff subsequently worked with FIND to submit a second application in March 2026 requesting an additional $405,130. If awarded, the additional funding would increase the total FIND funding to $810,260, which is 50% of the estimated construction cost. FIND is anticipated to announce the grant awards in late September 2026.
Construction is anticipated to begin in early 2027, with the goal of completing the project prior to the September 30, 2027 expenditure deadline for the initial FIND grant.
title: Approval of Amendment No. 1 to Task Authorization No. 5 to Dredging & Marine Consultants, LLC for Day Dock at Riverwalk Park Bidding Assistance, Construction Management, and Inspection

attachments.name: First Amendment to the Billboard Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement

description:
In accordance with Chapter 15 of the City’s Land Development Code (LDC), Lamar Outdoor Advertising (Lamar) is requesting approval of the First Amendment to the Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement for the relocation and reconstruction of existing billboard structures along I-95 and Ridgewood Avenue.
In 2025, the City Council approved a Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement with Lamar Outdoor Advertising to allow for the following changes:Southbound I-95 On-Ramp: The existing structure adjacent to the southbound I-95 on-ramp (5889 S. Williamson Boulevard), which currently contains one static sign face, will be removed and replaced with a new structure containing one digital sign face. In exchange, two existing sign faces will be permanently removed: one from the same parcel at 5889 S. Williamson Boulevard and one from 4901 S. Williamson Boulevard.
5865 Ridgewood Avenue: The existing structure, which currently contains four static sign faces, will be removed and replaced with a new structure featuring two digital sign faces, one oriented north and one oriented south. Landscaping will also be installed around the base of the structure. The installation, ongoing maintenance, and any necessary replacement of the landscaping will be the responsibility of Lamar Outdoor Advertising.
As part of the First Amendment to the Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement, Lamar Outdoor Advertising is requesting modifications to the structures previously approved under the 2025 agreement. The proposed modifications, which are in accordance with the requirements of Chapter 15 of the LDC and the proposed text amendments to Chapter 15 included in Ordinance No. 2026-9, which is also on this agenda for second reading, are as follows:Southbound I-95 On-Ramp (5889 S. Williamson Boulevard): The replacement structure would be 30 feet tall, an increase from the 25-foot height previously approved under the 2025 agreement.
Concept photo of a proposed 30-foot-tall structure at the I-95 southbound on-ramp location.
5865 Ridgewood Avenue (See Exhibit D): Each digital sign face would measure 380 square feet, an increase from the 246-square-foot sign faces previously approved under the 2025 agreement.
Concept photo of the proposed structure with one digital sign face on each side, where the proposed digital sign face area does not exceed the maximum allowable digital sign face area of 380 square feet.
Digital Billboard Lighting Standards: The First Amendment would clarify the applicable lighting requirements for digital billboards under the LDC. The LDC establishes two separate lighting standards applicable to digital billboard signs. The First Amendment would incorporate and clarify the applicability of both existing LDC lighting standards to the digital billboards subject to the Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement. No new lighting standard is being established through the First Amendment.Foot-Candle Requirement: Chapter 15 of the LDC establishes a maximum illumination level of 0.3 foot-candles above ambient light for digital signs. The provision also establishes a measurement procedure for determining compliance, including measuring ambient light with the sign turned off and the sign’s light output with the sign displaying a solid white image. The difference between the two measurements shall not exceed 0.3 foot-candles. The measurement distance is determined based on the sign area using the formula provided in the LDC.
NITS Requirement: Chapter 15 of the LDC also establishes an additional lighting standard specifically applicable to digital billboards. This provision regulates the LED display's brightness by establishing maximum daytime and nighttime levels. The NITS requirement was added to the LDC in 2025 and does not replace, remove, or modify the existing foot-candle requirement. This is a separate additional requirement.
No other changes to the terms, conditions, or requirements of the 2025 Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement are proposed in Lamar's requested First Amendment.
title: Approval of the First Amendment to the Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement with Lamar Outdoor Advertising

description:
On January 17, 2023, City Council approved Resolution No. 23-02 authorizing the execution of a Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Locally Funded Agreement (LFA) for the design of the Dunlawton Turn Lanes Bundle (FDOT Financial Project #449770; City of Port Orange Project CD215) utilizing FDOT District 5's continuing services design consultant, Dewberry Engineering, Inc. (Dewberry). The design plans were completed and approved by FDOT in January, 2025.
The Dunlawton Turn Lanes Bundle project consists of four (4) new turn lanes, three (3) extensions to existing turn lanes, and pedestrian improvements at intersections along the Dunlawton Avenue corridor to improve intersection capacity, reduce traffic delays, and enhance pedestrian safety. The proposed improvements include: 1. Eastbound right turn lane on Dunlawton Avenue at Clyde Morris Boulevard.
2. Westbound right turn lane on Dunlawton Avenue at City Center Parkway.
3. Westbound right turn lane on Dunlawton Avenue at Nova Road.
4. Eastbound right-turn lane on Yorktowne Boulevard at Dunlawton Avenue.
5. Extension of the existing westbound left-turn lane on Yorktowne Boulevard at Dunlawton Avenue.
6. Extension of the existing eastbound left-turn lane on Dunlawton Avenue at Nova Road.
7. Extension of the existing westbound left-turn lane on Dunlawton Avenue at Clyde Morris Boulevard.
During the design phase, it was determined that two of the proposed turn lane improvements (Turn Lanes #1 and #3 described above) require the acquisition of additional right-of-way or easement for construction. The project is currently in the Right-of-Way phase, as approved by City Council at the May 5, 2026 meeting, with concurrence from FDOT. The City's right-of-way consultant is currently working to acquire the necessary right-of-way or easement. The project is fully funded for construction in FDOT's Fiscal Year 2026/2027 work program, with construction anticipated to begin in Spring 2027. The time frame between FDOT's concurrence of the design plans and May 2026 is attributed to coordination with FDOT regarding approval of the right-of-way phase of the project and securing a right-of-way consultant qualified for compliance with FDOT’s Right of Way Procedures Manual and the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act of 1970.
According to FDOT's procedures, once the required right-of-way or easements have been acquired, the 2025 design plans must be updated to incorporate the acquired right-of-way and easement areas and revised to comply with the current FDOT Fiscal Year 2026/27 design standards before construction begins.
FDOT's contract for design services with Dewberry is active until December 31, 2026. Therefore, to maintain design continuity and complete the required plan updates in the most economical manner, Staff requests approval of the Locally Funded Agreement with FDOT to engage Dewberry to perform the required plan update/post design services for the project they designed in 2025. The estimate of cost for the plan update/post design services is $4,796.35 which the City will fully fund. The Locally Funded Agreement stipulates that the City shall furnish to the FDOT an advance deposit in the amount of $4,797.00 within fourteen (14) calendar days of the execution of the agreement. The payment of funds under the Locally Funded Agreement will be made directly to FDOT as provided in the attached Three Party Escrow Agreement. Funds are budgeted and available in CD215 for this purpose. Dewberry anticipates completing the required plan updates by the end of 2026, allowing the project to proceed to construction as scheduled.
title: Resolution No. 26-38 - Approval of Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) Locally Funded Agreement and associated Three Party Escrow Agreement to utilize Dewberry Engineering for plan update/post design services for the Dunlawton Avenue Turn Lanes Bundle Project (FDOT 449770-2-58/68) - Port Orange Project CD215

description:
In July 2026, the City received the draft grant agreement from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) for the legislative appropriations grant in the amount of $1,232,500 to fund the Portona Stormwater Ponds and Infrastructure Upgrades Project.
The project area is located within one of the City's older neighborhoods, where many homes were constructed in the 1970s, prior to the City's adoption of modern stormwater management requirements in the early 1990s. As a result, the area has experienced significant flooding, including during Hurricanes Ian and Milton. The proposed improvements are intended to reduce the risk of structural flooding during hurricanes and other severe rainfall events, thereby enhancing the neighborhood's overall resilience to stormwater impacts.
The project scope includes the construction of a new stormwater pond, installation of new stormwater pipes and inlets to convey runoff to the pond, and installation of a backflow prevention device at an existing outfall beneath the Florida East Coast (FEC) railroad tracks. These improvements will enhance drainage capacity, reduce flood risk, and increase the overall resilience of the surrounding neighborhood.

description:
The adopted FY 25-26 budget includes approximately $15 million for city-wide fleet replacement and additions. About two thirds of this cost was planned to be funded with debt and the remaining funds are included in the fleet fund and other sources. Debt funding in the current Fiscal Year (FY) was planned only for higher cost items such as fire trucks, ambulances, and larger stormwater equipment. The City has utilized debt financing for less expensive fleet replacement, such as police vehicles, in the past. That practice has been discontinued, and those items will be purchased under the more traditional fleet replacement fund going forward.
In prior years, the City borrowed fleet funds from banks. For the current FY, Staff recommends financing these items by borrowing from the Utilities unrestricted fund balance and repaying it with interest at the rate it is generally earning as invested (3%). This option would lower overall costs based on slightly lower interest rates and no processing and closing costs. It would also reduce the complexity of the process. This option will not impact the health of the utility fund as it represents only about a third of the current fund balance and it will be fully repaid so the reserves will be available as intended to support the utilities fund if needed during construction of the Water Reclamation Facility upgrades and other future capital projects.
title: Resolution No. 26-45 - Approval of Interfund Loans from Public Utilities to finance the acquisition of Fleet vehicles and equipment

description:
This resolution adopts the Non-Ad Valorem Assessment Roll for Fiscal Year 2027 and approves the current stormwater utility fee rate with no rate change from the prior fiscal year. Pursuant to Section 197.3632, Florida Statutes, the City must certify the assessment roll (list of parcels) to the Volusia County Tax Collector each year to facilitate collection of the stormwater utility fee through the uniform method of collection, so that the assessment is included on the annual property tax bill.
The resolution approves the current stormwater fee rate schedule previously approved by City Resolution No. 23-21, including a maximum rate of $160 per Equivalent Dwelling Unit (EDU) for Fiscal Year 2027. One EDU is equivalent to 3,050 square feet of impervious surface, with residential properties generally assigned one EDU per dwelling unit and non-residential properties assessed based on impervious surface area.
Approval of this resolution will also authorize the Finance Director to certify and deliver the Fiscal Year 2027 Non-Ad Valorem Assessment Roll to the Volusia County Tax Collector by September 15, 2026, as required for collection on the annual property tax bill. ​

description:
Planning Commission Recommendation (6-25-26): Recommended Approval 3-2
This agenda item is a Land Development Code (LDC) amendment initiated by Lamar Company L.L.C. (Lamar Outdoor Advertising) to make changes to Chapter 15 of the City’s LDC relating to billboards. According to Lamar, the proposed text amendment is intended to modify the dimensional requirements for digital sign faces applicable to reconstructed billboards, specifically the allowable height of the billboard structure and the size of the digital sign face.
In 2025, Lamar requested a text amendment to Chapter 15 of the Land Development Code (LDC) that established a process for replacing existing static billboard sign faces with digital (LED) sign faces. The amendment also established additional standards and requirements specifically applicable to the reconstruction of billboard sign faces as digital (LED) sign faces, in addition to the other applicable regulations for digital signs contained in Chapter 15 of the LDC.
The 2025 amendment was initiated by Lamar to modernize select existing billboard locations while reducing the overall number of billboard sign faces in the city. The 2025 amendment established criteria for billboard reconstruction along Ridgewood Avenue and I-95 and required the removal of at least two (2) existing static billboard sign faces within the City for each reconstructed digital sign face. The 2025 amendment also requires a Billboard Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement for each reconstruction project. The agreement identifies the existing static billboard sign faces to be removed and the location where the replacement digital sign face will be constructed. The agreement also establishes the specific terms and conditions for the relocation and reconstruction of the billboard based on the requirements of the LDC and requires City Council approval.
According to Lamar, the proposed amendment is intended to clarify existing standards and enable the constructability of proposed digital sign face replacements. During the review of permit applications for two (2) proposed billboard reconstruction projects, the applicant determined that the current standards adopted in 2025 limited the design of the replacement billboards and digital sign faces. Therefore, Lamar is requesting amendments to Chapter 15, Sections 14 and 16 of the LDC, as follows:
1. Height Standard: The current LDC limits the height of a reconstructed billboard to the height of the existing billboard being removed from the same property. The applicant proposes revising this standard to allow a reconstructed billboard to be no taller than the height of the existing billboard or 30 feet, whichever is greater. This would establish a minimum allowable height of 30 feet for reconstructed billboards, regardless of the height of the existing billboard being removed.
The applicant states that, at lower heights, maintenance of a digital sign face would require a “shepherd’s hook” anchorage device, which could potentially damage the digital sign face and is inconsistent with Lamar’s preferred maintenance practices. Lamar further states that the requested modification would allow the maintenance platforms (catwalks) to be positioned to provide adequate clearance above ground level, improving worker safety and eliminating the need for equipment that could potentially damage the digital sign face. According to Lamar, the requested modification is intended to establish a minimum height of 30 feet above ground level (HAGL) to facilitate the safe installation, maintenance, and servicing of the billboard structure.
2. Digital Sign Face Area: The current LDC limits the size of a reconstructed digital sign face to the square footage of the largest single static sign face removed as part of the approved sign face exchange. Lamar is requesting to revise this requirement to allow the size of the reconstructed digital sign face to be based on the combined area of all static sign faces removed from the same property that are oriented in the same direction, subject to a maximum digital sign face area of 380 square feet.
For example, under the current LDC requirement, if two (2) static sign faces on the same structure are oriented in the same direction and each measures 246 square feet, the maximum allowable reconstructed digital sign face would be 246 square feet because the current standard is based on the largest individual static sign face removed. Under the proposed amendment, the combined area of the two removed sign faces would be 492 square feet or a maximum allowable digital sign face of 380 square feet, whichever is less.
Lamar states that approximately 380 square feet is the minimum LED display size readily available from its manufacturer. As a result, the applicant indicates that the current standard limits reconstruction at certain locations to approximately 246 square feet, which is not sufficient to accommodate the available LED display technology.
Example of a structure with more than one sign oriented in the same direction with a sign area of 246 square feet for each sign face.
Example of a billboard structure with one digital sign face on each side, where the proposed digital sign face area exceeds the combined area of the two removed static sign faces (246 square feet each) but does not exceed the maximum allowable digital sign face area of 380 square feet.
3. Removal Requirement: The current LDC requires the structure and sign faces to be removed prior to issuance of a building permit for a reconstructed billboard. Lamar is requesting that this requirement be revised to allow the demolition permit for the existing structure and sign faces, and the building permit for the reconstructed structure and digital sign face, to be issued at the same time. According to Lamar, the proposed change is intended to allow the demolition and new construction permits to be processed and issued concurrently. This request is consistent with the City's permitting for other demolition and redevelopment projects, such as demolishing an existing home and constructing a new home on the same property.
If the proposed LDC amendments are approved, Lamar intends to request City Council approval for an amendment to the approved 2025 Billboard Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement to amend the following reconstruction projects:
1. Ridgewood Avenue/Nova Road: Removal of a 34.5-foot-tall billboard structure with four (4) static sign faces, each measuring 246 square feet, located north of the intersection of Ridgewood Avenue and Nova Road. The applicant proposes to reconstruct a digital billboard at the same location, maintaining the existing 34.5-foot height, with two (2) digital sign faces, each measuring 378 square feet.
Photo of sign to be rebuilt with one sign face per side with a sign area of 378 square feet
2. I-95/Williamson Boulevard: Removal of a 25-foot-tall billboard structure with a 464-square-foot static sign face located along the I-95 southbound on-ramp near the Dunlawton Avenue/Taylor Road interchange (5889 Williamson Boulevard), and removal of a 23-foot-tall billboard structure with a 527-square-foot static sign face located along northbound I-95 south of the Williamson Boulevard overpass (4901 Williamson Boulevard). The applicant proposes to reconstruct a 30-foot-tall digital billboard at the I-95 southbound location with a 464-square-foot digital sign face.
Concept Photo of a 30-foot-tall digital billboard at the I-95 southbound location.

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (August 27, 2026): Recommended ​Approval ​4-0
The subject property is located at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard, at the northwest corner of Clyde Morris Boulevard and Dunlawton Avenue, and is part of the Robinson Planned Commercial Development (PCD), which was approved by the Port Orange City Council in 1987. The Robinson PCD established the permitted uses and building dimensional requirements applicable to the development of the subject property. The subject property was developed as a bank in 1989 and operated as a bank for approximately 37 years. The site has been vacant for approximately five years.
Location map of 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard
According to the property owner/applicant, the requested changes to the Master Development Agreement (MDA) for the Robinson PCD would allow the existing bank drive-thru canopy to be enclosed and converted into additional office space, which would be incorporated into the existing building. If approved, the vacant bank building would be redeveloped as a dental office for White Wolf Dental. The proposed redevelopment of the building and site would include interior and exterior renovations to the existing building, enclosure of the existing drive-thru canopy, and installation of new landscaping throughout the site.
The property owner/applicant requests the following amendments to the MDA for the Robinson PCD based on the redevelopment plan for the building and site:To reduce the internal side yard setback from 15 feet to 10 feet. The requested 10-foot side yard building setback is consistent with the current standard side yard building setback requirements in the Land Development Code (LDC) for comparable City zoning districts that allow office and institutional uses, such as Professional Office, Neighborhood Commercial, Office/Residential Transition, and Government/Public Use. The requested 10-foot side-yard building setback is consistent with current side-yard building setback requirements in other non-residential zoning districts that support office uses.
To remove the 75-foot building separation requirement and allow the building separation to be as required by the Florida Building Code (FBC) and National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). Current City dimensional standards for commercial and office zoning districts in Chapter 17 of the LDC do not establish a specific building separation requirement; instead, building separation is determined based on required setbacks and compliance with the FBC and NFPA standards. Consistent with the City's current development review process, building separation is evaluated based on compliance with applicable FBC and NFPA requirements rather than on a city-established building separation standard. The proposed amendment would remove the building separation requirement from the MDA and allow the lot to be redeveloped in a manner consistent with the applicable FBC and NFPA requirements, as well as the side setbacks established for the subject and adjacent properties. If the MDA amendment is approved, the side yard building setback for the property at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard would be reduced to 10 feet. The adjacent property to the south has a required minimum side-yard building setback of 15 feet, with an actual setback of approximately 26 feet. Therefore, the separation between the building on the adjacent property to the south of the subject property and the enclosed bank canopy would be 36 feet, which exceeds the applicable building separation requirements under the FBC and NFPA standards, which require a separation of greater than 10 feet.
Picture of the existing building at 4900 Clyde Morris Boulevard shows the canopy area to be enclosed and the adjacent office to the south, with the proposed building separation labeled.
The staff report is attached for more detail.

description:
Currently, the Code of Ordinances provides a three-day limit for setup and take-down before and after a Special Event. The Code also provides a process for City Council to approve an extended timeframe when setup and take-down activities exceed the three-day limitation.
The Code of Ordinances states that Special Events associated with a legal holiday or seasonal event, such as spring landscaping, Christmas tree sales, Halloween pumpkin sales, or sparkler sales, shall not exceed forty (40) consecutive calendar days and are limited to three (3) days prior to the event for setup and three (3) days after the event for take-down.
In recent years, some seasonal events have required additional setup and take-down time due to operational requirements. For example, last year, Home Depot and Lowe’s were approved for an additional 30 days of setup/take-down time outside the actual event timeframe [e.g. Special Event ran from November 15, 2025, through December 24, 2025 (39 days); the tent and sales area set-up begin on October 24, 2025, and was completed November 14, 2025 (21 days); take-down was completed on January 2, 2026 (9 days)]. These requirements may include tent and electrical installation and inspection, the setup of seasonal merchandise (Christmas trees, pumpkins, etc.), internal business or tenant procedures for preparing and closing the site for sales, and scheduling the removal of tents or other rented structures.
After several years of requests for extended setup and take-down periods being brought before and approved by City Council for seasonal events, Staff is proposing an amendment to Chapter 58, Article III, Special Events, Section 58-53.
The proposed amendment would allow additional setup and take-down time beyond the three-day limitation for seasonal events involving the sale of seasonal merchandise, such as Christmas trees and pumpkins, to be approved by the Administrative Official. Approval would be based on a determination that the additional time requested is justified by the operational circumstances of the event. This may include the time reasonably necessary for the delivery, placement, setup, or removal of equipment, tents, inventory, displays, or similar materials.
The proposed amendment would also include language requiring tents, other temporary structures, and merchandise associated with the event to be secured or removed in the event of an approaching hurricane, tropical storm, or other significant weather event.
If the Administrative Official does not approve the requested additional time for setup and takedown before and after a Special Event, the applicant may still request approval from the City Council.

description:
The Florida Legislature passed major regulatory reforms during the 2026 legislative session, which will fundamentally shift how municipal wastewater utilities manage and dispose of sewage sludge. Most notably, a provision embedded in the 2026 Florida Farm Bill institutes a statewide ban on the land application of Class B biosolids by 2028. This legislation will significantly increase operating and hauling costs for utilities across the state.
The City is coming to the end of a 10-year contract with Shelly's Environmental for biosolids hauling and disposal. Staff has contacted local municipalities with newer biosolids contracts and pricing is ranging from $175 per wet/ton to $250 per wet/ton. The City is currently paying $102 per wet/ton. With the recent passing of legislation, the market price is expected to be much higher in the coming years. In anticipation of the biosolids legislation and major price increases, Staff met with Volusia County Staff last year and started the initial discussions of a potential regional biosolids facility on jointly owned property. The County has agreed to pay 50% of the costs associated with the evaluation and a formal Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the County is on this agenda for Council consideration.
The City has requested that Kimley-Horn provide engineering services to evaluate multiple proposed sites located adjacent to the Volusia County Landfill.
The following will be considered for this biosolids evaluation study:Evaluate up to three treatment technologies for biosolids processing.
Evaluate the viability of the proposed sites, including regulatory, water quality, environmental impacts to neighbors, including odor and traffic, and facility operations requirements.
Review and evaluate local municipalities’ biosolids data to support the proposed regional biosolids facility.
Review and compile proposed capital and net operating costs for each treatment technology.
Review and identify potential state grants and private funding sources.
title: Approval of Task Authorization No. 31 with Kimley-Horn for a Port Orange Regional Biosolids Evaluation Study in the amount of $98,824.00

description:
Due to the increased regulatory restrictions and escalating operating costs associated with biosolids land application, the City, in conjunction with Volusia County (“County”), is requesting approval of this Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Volusia County for a Biosolids Facility Feasibility Analysis (“Study”). The proposed Study would evaluate the needs, regulatory constraints, and costs associated with a regional biosolids facility. The Study will assess the feasibility of building a facility located on jointly owned property adjacent to the County landfill where recovered methane gas would be available for sludge drying operations. Currently, the recovered methane gas is being flared off into the atmosphere. The Study would evaluate whether the recovered methane could generate enough BTU's to operate a sludge drying facility.
A scope of work, attached to the MOU, marked Exhibit A, will be performed by the City’s engineering consultant (and mutually agreed upon by the County). There are no direct costs associated with this MOU, and any costs incurred with the performance of the Study will be related to the City Task Authorization issued to its engineering consultant (“Contractor”) to perform the Study. Pursuant to the MOU, the County will reimburse the City one-half (i.e. 50%) of all compensation paid to the Contractor by the City in connection with the Study, including one-half (i.e. 50%) of any Study amounts the City may pay in excess of the Contractor’s estimate provided in Exhibit A, attached to the MOU.
title: Approval of Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Volusia County for a Biosolids Facility Feasibility Analysis
