description:
Planning Commission Recommendation (6-25-26): Recommended Approval 3-2
This agenda item is a Land Development Code (LDC) amendment initiated by Lamar Company L.L.C. (Lamar Outdoor Advertising) to make changes to Chapter 15 of the City’s LDC relating to billboards. According to Lamar, the proposed text amendment is intended to modify the dimensional requirements for digital sign faces applicable to reconstructed billboards, specifically the allowable height of the billboard structure and the size of the digital sign face.
In 2025, Lamar requested a text amendment to Chapter 15 of the Land Development Code (LDC) that established a process for replacing existing static billboard sign faces with digital (LED) sign faces. The amendment also established additional standards and requirements specifically applicable to the reconstruction of billboard sign faces as digital (LED) sign faces, in addition to the other applicable regulations for digital signs contained in Chapter 15 of the LDC.
The 2025 amendment was initiated by Lamar to modernize select existing billboard locations while reducing the overall number of billboard sign faces in the city. The 2025 amendment established criteria for billboard reconstruction along Ridgewood Avenue and I-95 and required the removal of at least two (2) existing static billboard sign faces within the City for each reconstructed digital sign face. The 2025 amendment also requires a Billboard Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement for each reconstruction project. The agreement identifies the existing static billboard sign faces to be removed and the location where the replacement digital sign face will be constructed. The agreement also establishes the specific terms and conditions for the relocation and reconstruction of the billboard based on the requirements of the LDC and requires City Council approval.
According to Lamar, the proposed amendment is intended to clarify existing standards and enable the constructability of proposed digital sign face replacements. During the review of permit applications for two (2) proposed billboard reconstruction projects, the applicant determined that the current standards adopted in 2025 limited the design of the replacement billboards and digital sign faces. Therefore, Lamar is requesting amendments to Chapter 15, Sections 14 and 16 of the LDC, as follows:
1. Height Standard: The current LDC limits the height of a reconstructed billboard to the height of the existing billboard being removed from the same property. The applicant proposes revising this standard to allow a reconstructed billboard to be no taller than the height of the existing billboard or 30 feet, whichever is greater. This would establish a minimum allowable height of 30 feet for reconstructed billboards, regardless of the height of the existing billboard being removed.
The applicant states that, at lower heights, maintenance of a digital sign face would require a “shepherd’s hook” anchorage device, which could potentially damage the digital sign face and is inconsistent with Lamar’s preferred maintenance practices. Lamar further states that the requested modification would allow the maintenance platforms (catwalks) to be positioned to provide adequate clearance above ground level, improving worker safety and eliminating the need for equipment that could potentially damage the digital sign face. According to Lamar, the requested modification is intended to establish a minimum height of 30 feet above ground level (HAGL) to facilitate the safe installation, maintenance, and servicing of the billboard structure.
2. Digital Sign Face Area: The current LDC limits the size of a reconstructed digital sign face to the square footage of the largest single static sign face removed as part of the approved sign face exchange. Lamar is requesting to revise this requirement to allow the size of the reconstructed digital sign face to be based on the combined area of all static sign faces removed from the same property that are oriented in the same direction, subject to a maximum digital sign face area of 380 square feet.
For example, under the current LDC requirement, if two (2) static sign faces on the same structure are oriented in the same direction and each measures 246 square feet, the maximum allowable reconstructed digital sign face would be 246 square feet because the current standard is based on the largest individual static sign face removed. Under the proposed amendment, the combined area of the two removed sign faces would be 492 square feet or a maximum allowable digital sign face of 380 square feet, whichever is less.
Lamar states that approximately 380 square feet is the minimum LED display size readily available from its manufacturer. As a result, the applicant indicates that the current standard limits reconstruction at certain locations to approximately 246 square feet, which is not sufficient to accommodate the available LED display technology.
Example of a structure with more than one sign oriented in the same direction with a sign area of 246 square feet for each sign face.
Example of a billboard structure with one digital sign face on each side, where the proposed digital sign face area exceeds the combined area of the two removed static sign faces (246 square feet each) but does not exceed the maximum allowable digital sign face area of 380 square feet.
3. Removal Requirement: The current LDC requires the structure and sign faces to be removed prior to issuance of a building permit for a reconstructed billboard. Lamar is requesting that this requirement be revised to allow the demolition permit for the existing structure and sign faces, and the building permit for the reconstructed structure and digital sign face, to be issued at the same time. According to Lamar, the proposed change is intended to allow the demolition and new construction permits to be processed and issued concurrently. This request is consistent with the City's permitting for other demolition and redevelopment projects, such as demolishing an existing home and constructing a new home on the same property.
If the proposed LDC amendments are approved, Lamar intends to request City Council approval for an amendment to the approved 2025 Billboard Relocation and Reconstruction Agreement to amend the following reconstruction projects:
1. Ridgewood Avenue/Nova Road: Removal of a 34.5-foot-tall billboard structure with four (4) static sign faces, each measuring 246 square feet, located north of the intersection of Ridgewood Avenue and Nova Road. The applicant proposes to reconstruct a digital billboard at the same location, maintaining the existing 34.5-foot height, with two (2) digital sign faces, each measuring 378 square feet.
Photo of sign to be rebuilt with one sign face per side with a sign area of 378 square feet
2. I-95/Williamson Boulevard: Removal of a 25-foot-tall billboard structure with a 464-square-foot static sign face located along the I-95 southbound on-ramp near the Dunlawton Avenue/Taylor Road interchange (5889 Williamson Boulevard), and removal of a 23-foot-tall billboard structure with a 527-square-foot static sign face located along northbound I-95 south of the Williamson Boulevard overpass (4901 Williamson Boulevard). The applicant proposes to reconstruct a 30-foot-tall digital billboard at the I-95 southbound location with a 464-square-foot digital sign face.
Concept Photo of a 30-foot-tall digital billboard at the I-95 southbound location.

The University of North Florida Training and Services, Institute Inc., d/b/a Institute of Police Technology and Management (IPTM) received a Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) grant for Florida's Bicycle Pedestrian Focused Initiative: Communication and High Visibility and Enforcement Project. The subcontract between IPTM and the City in the amount of $17,806.48 encompasses a project that will utilize law enforcement staff to reinforce safe pedestrian, bicyclist, and driver behavior in priority counties. The goal of the effort is to reduce traffic crashes resulting in serious and fatal injuries to pedestrians and bicyclists using high-visibility education and enforcement details. This reimbursement contract will cover project expenses, including overtime hours for sworn law enforcement officers.
The grant aims to develop and implement effective community-level high-visibility education and enforcement details in areas with the highest representation of traffic crashes resulting in serious and fatal injuries to pedestrians and bicyclists. The goal is to mitigate crashes by increasing awareness of the laws and compliance with traffic laws that protect the safety of pedestrians and bicyclists by providing high-visibility education and enforcement of all road users (pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorists) to change behaviors and improve safety. The Police Department will conduct on-street education and enforcement details at pre-approved locations within pre-approved times and distribute educational materials with each contact.
The Police Department will use the funds to provide additional high-visibility patrols to focus on pedestrian, bicycle, and crosswalk safety violations through education and enforcement. Personnel assigned to this initiative will be paid overtime and will not affect minimum patrol staffing levels. Staff participating in this program will receive the required training.

description:
In 1981, the City established Chapter 82, Article II regarding the use, operation and mooring of watercraft within the City of Port Orange. In 1998, the City adopted Ordinance No. 1998-11 establishing Sections 82-44 through 82-45 of the Code of Ordinances providing for the mooring of vessels in waters of the city, and the impoundment of vessels.
Recently, the Florida legislature adopted Senate Bill 164, and House Bill 481, enacting new regulations regarding anchoring and mooring prohibitions. The proposed amendment to the Code of Ordinances reflects the recent changes adopted by the Florida legislature. The proposed Ordinance expands on the process for impounding vessels, the establishment for impoundment hearings, and provides parameters for the use of City-owned docks and boat ramps, including limitations on the duration of time in which individuals may dock. Additionally, the proposed Ordinance also details specific provisions for live-aboard vessels and commercial vessels, including a maximum period of time in which they may anchor or moor in city waters. Overall, the changes in the proposed Ordinance are intended to bring the City's code up to date with the current statutory provisions, and provide mechanisms for addressing vessels moored or anchored in city waters in violation of City Code.

description:
The proposed ordinance amends Chapter 2, Administration, Article III, Boards and Commissions, Division 4, Environmental Advisory Board, Sections 2-118, 2-119, and 2-121 of the City Code to reduce the membership of the Environmental Advisory Board from seven (7) members to five (5) members, revise the Board’s initial appointment structure to reflect the reduced membership, and update the quorum requirement consistent with the revised Board composition.
At the April 26, 2026, Environmental Advisory Board (EAB) meeting, staff discussed the proposed change in membership from seven (7) members to five (5) members. The EAB supported the proposed amendment to reduce the number of Board members to five (5).
Over the past two (2) years, the Board has typically had one to two (1–2) vacancies at any given time, making it difficult to consistently achieve a quorum and conduct meetings. Reducing the Board membership to five (5) members is intended to better align the Board’s structure with current participation levels and improve the likelihood of maintaining a full membership. This adjustment is expected to improve quorum reliability and enhance the Board’s ability to conduct business and provide timely input and recommendations to the City Council.
The ordinance also updates the Environmental Advisory Board’s organizational provisions to align with the revised five-member Board structure, including changes to the Board’s membership composition, appointment schedule, and quorum requirements.
Section 2-118 is revised to establish the Environmental Advisory Board as a five (5)-member board.
Section 2-119 is revised to establish a staggered appointment structure consistent with a five-member Board. The appointments will include two (2) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2027, and three (3) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2030. Pursuant to the City Code, Environmental Advisory Board members serve three (3)-year terms, with all terms expiring in May of the applicable year. Members are eligible for reappointment for any number of consecutive terms.
Section 2-121 is revised to modify the quorum requirement consistent with the reduced Board membership. The amendment changes the quorum requirement from four (4) members to three (3) members, allowing the five-member Board to conduct official business with a majority of appointed members present.

The requested time extension will allow for the completion of this additional scope of work while ensuring the City receives the full operational benefits of the facility improvements.
The facility will also serve as a centralized storage location for materials and equipment used in sandbag filling and distribution operations. Due to its proximity to the City’s Disaster Debris Management Site (DDMS) and designated sandbag distribution area, the Storage Building will enhance interdepartmental coordination and improve the City’s ability to respond efficiently and effectively to weather-related emergencies.

description:
Due to the size, complexity, and critical operational role of vertical turbine pumps used at the City's water and wastewater facilities, obtaining multiple competitive bids is often impractical and cost-prohibitive. These highly specialized pumps are integral components of the City's utility infrastructure. Typically manufactured by industry-specific providers such as Pentair, Layne-Vertiline, and Ingersoll Rand. The pumps generally range from 18 to 24 feet in length with a new purchase price of approximately $200,000 and an average rebuild costing approximately $75,000.
Accurate evaluation and repair quotations require the pumps to be removed from service, transported to a qualified repair facility, fully disassembled, and inspected. This process involves specialized equipment, including cranes for extraction and reinstallation, resulting in significant labor, transportation costs, and system downtime. Onsite evaluation of these pumps is not feasible due to the specialized tools, disassembly devices, and large housing facility. Repeating this process with multiple vendors solely to satisfy formal bidding requirements would substantially increase costs, extend outages, and jeopardize the reliable operation of essential utility services.
Accordingly, Staff recommends waiving formal bidding requirements for the repair of these vertical turbine pumps when necessary, as the logistical and financial burden of obtaining multiple bids outweighs the potential benefit. This approach will allow the City to utilize qualified vendors capable of providing timely and reliable repair services, minimizing service disruptions and protecting critical infrastructure.
Staff further recommends authorizing the City Manager and City Attorney to approve contract documents and authorize the City Manager to execute all task authorizations, purchase orders, change orders, and other documents necessary to facilitate these repair services, subject to appropriated budget.

title: Request to Waive Formal Bidding for Vertical Turbine Pumps at the Water & Wastewater Treatment Facilities

description:
As a recipient of the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), the City of Port Orange is eligible for annual allocations to support an approved 5-Year Consolidated Plan. The Annual Action Plan serves as the City’s application for the eligible annual funding, and describes needs, goals, and objectives supporting the 5-Year Consolidated Plan.
The new 5-Year Consolidated Plan will run from 2026-2030. Developing the 5-Year Consolidated Plan includes a needs assessment, market analysis, and developing a strategic plan for the utilization of these funds. Comments were accepted until July 17, 2026. The PY2026 allocation is $376,501 and the proposed Annual Action Plan activities are: 1) White Place Park Revitalization ($301,201) and 2) Planning & Administration ($75,300).

description: In 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 2024-22, implementing a negotiated pension enhancement for members of the Fire Pension. Shortly thereafter, questions arose regarding whether the 300 hours of pensionable OT includes the built-in OT that each firefighter earns as part of the traditional 2,912 hour (24-on / 24-off) shift work – approximately 250 hours each year. description:
Note: Summary and Ordinance have been updated from the June 18, 2026 original.
At the June 18 meeting, City Council approved Ordinance No. 2026-08 on first reading, subject to the following revisions:The minimum lot width requirement for detached single-family residential lots within the Community District shall remain 50 feet.
The reference in Figure 17.1 to a density of 16 dwelling units per acre for the 14-acre tract of land has been revised to 8 dwelling units per acre, and Figure 17.2 has been updated to depict the 14-acre tract within the Community District.
The attached Ordinance No. 2026-08 has been revised to incorporate these Council-directed changes.
The original Summary with an updated map is below.
Planning Commission Recommendation (5-28-26): Recommended Approval 5-0
The applicant, Jessica Gow, Esq., on behalf of property owner FL P70 LLC, requests an amendment to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the Land Development Code (LDC) for the Planned Community-Agriculture (PC-A) zoning district. The 1,201-acre PC-A zoning district was established by the City Council in 2002 to support the development of a mixed-use community on the west side of Port Orange. The PC-A zoning district is generally located between Interstate 95 and Tomoka Farms Road, south of the FPL Easement.
Location Map of the PC—A Zoning District
According to the applicant, the proposed text amendments are to update the PC-A zoning district regulations to support continued development of this area in response to existing market demand, by revising the locations of where uses are allowed to be developed within the PC-A while remaining consistent with the current Planned Community-Westside Future Land Use designation, along with minor clean-up revisions, and clarifications to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the LDC.
The PC-A zoning district is required to remain consistent with the underlying Future Land Use (FLU) designation in the Comprehensive Plan for the 1,201-acre PC-A area known as the Planned Community–Westside FLU designation. The Planned Community–Westside FLU designation was adopted in 2002 (formerly known as Planned Community No. 1) along with the PC-A zoning district. The FLU designation establishes the overall development framework for the area, including the following limits and requirements:Maximum overall gross residential density of up to 4 dwelling units per acre (approximately 4,804 total units), with higher densities permitted in designated mixed-use areas, provided the overall density cap of 4 dwelling units per acre is maintained.
The required land use mix, within the PC-A area, shall be within the following range upon buildout:Residential: 35% – 60%
Commercial: 10% – 25%
Industrial: 10% – 25%
Mixed-use town center: 10% – 25%
Conservation/recreation: minimum 10%
Daily Trip cap of 62,600 average daily vehicle trips per day within the PC-A.
Development pattern supporting a central town center, internal connectivity for vehicles and pedestrians, and a transition from higher-intensity uses near Interstate 95 to lower-intensity uses toward the site's outer areas.
Any proposed changes to the PC-A zoning district must remain consistent with the underlying Future Land Use (FLU) designation. The proposed amendment does not change the FLU designation or the limits and development requirements in the Comprehensive Plan for this 1,201-acre property.
According to the applicant, regional development patterns in Volusia County, particularly in the Port Orange and Daytona Beach area, have changed significantly since the PC-A district was originally established about 25 years ago, in 2002. At that time, the PC-A was intended to accommodate a broader mix of employment-based and industrial uses; however, many traditional manufacturing uses have since declined or transitioned toward logistics and distribution-based operations.
Modern industrial and commercial development is increasingly driven by e-commerce growth, demand for same-day and next-day delivery, and direct access to interstate corridors. Over the past several years, the I-4 and I-95 interchange area in Daytona Beach has become the primary location for large-scale warehouse and distribution centers, e-commerce fulfillment facilities, and industrial parks due to its regional connectivity and transportation advantages. In contrast, the PC-A has become less competitive for these uses due to its limited direct interstate access.
As a result, the applicant proposes adjusting the distribution of land uses within the PC-A in response to evolving market conditions while maintaining the overall mixed-use framework. Specifically, the applicant is requesting to reallocate approximately +/- 241 acres from the Workplace District, an employment-focused area intended for commercial and industrial development serving both local and regional markets, to the Community District, a transitional area primarily intended for residential uses, with supporting civic, recreational, and commercial uses.
The proposed amendments to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the Land Development Code (LDC) include: Figures 17.1 and 17.2 are revised to update the PC-A conceptual development plan in the northern area where vacant land remains. The primary change includes approximately +/- 241 acres shifting from the Workplace District to the Community District.
Duplicate and outdated text has been removed
Design standards and permitted uses have been cross-referenced to the appropriate Chapters of the LDC.
Added design flexibility through site plan review for future development in the West Town Center District
Allows development within the Community District to set aside open space areas outside a project's limit, subject to approval of a separate agreement by the City.
Current District Map for the PC-A
Proposed District Map for the PC-A
The applicant is also requesting a reduction in the minimum lot width from 50 feet to 40 feet for single-family lots in the Community District. No changes are proposed to the minimum lot area requirement of 5,000 square feet or to other dimensional standards, including open space, building and driveway setbacks, or depth of on-site parking area. The applicant states that a 40-foot-by-125-foot lot provides additional depth, which can improve layout flexibility compared to a 50-foot-by-100-foot lot. The added depth allows for more usable rear-yard space, greater flexibility in building placement, and the ability to accommodate rear-loaded garages, resulting in a different development pattern and street-facing design along the frontage. Even with a 40-foot-wide lot, typical lot layout, driveway placement, and required setbacks generally still provide sufficient space to accommodate at least one on-street parking space in front of a lot, in addition to the required driveway area.
According to the applicant, the proposed amendment is intended to provide greater flexibility in residential lot design and allow for a wider range of housing types and site layouts in this district. The applicant further indicates that the request is consistent with the intent of the Community District as described in the LDC as a transitional residential area located between the West Town Center District and the surrounding Neighborhood and Workplace Districts to support residential development with strong street frontage interaction, pedestrian connectivity, and integrated circulation networks, including sidewalks, bikeways, alleyways, and on-street parking.
Since 2002, about 610 acres of the 1,201-acre PC-A district have been developed or set aside for conservation. Most development has occurred in the southern part of the district and has been primarily residential. To date, about 452 acres have been developed for residential use, resulting in 2,167 homes (including both single-family and multifamily units).According to the Comprehensive Plan, no more than 721 acres of the PC-A district can be used for residential development, and the maximum gross residential density for the 1,201-acre PC-A district is 4 units per acre. Therefore, about 261 acres of the 1,201 acres could still be developed for residential use. Based on residential development over the last 25 years, developed residential areas average about 4.8 units per acre. If the remaining 261 acres are developed at a similar level, about 1,250 more residential units could be built. In total, the full build-out of the allowed residential development area (721 acres) within the 1,201-acre site would result in approximately 3,400 homes across the 1,201-acre PC-A district. This represents about 1,400 fewer homes than the maximum allowed under the Comprehensive Plan, resulting in an overall gross density of approximately 2.85 homes per acre across the 1,201-acre district.
Overall, the proposed amendment maintains all existing density and intensity (non-residential square footage) limits and does not increase the total average daily vehicle trips per day or the allowable residential or non-residential development beyond what was approved in 2002 with the adoption of the Planned Community–Westside FLU designation.
title: Second Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-8 - Amendments to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the Land Development Code (LDC) for the Planned Community-Agriculture (PC-A) zoning district (Case No. DCAM-25-0005)

description:
In 1981, the City established Chapter 82, Article II regarding the use, operation and mooring of watercraft within the City of Port Orange. In 1998, the City adopted Ordinance No. 1998-11 establishing Sections 82-44 through 82-45 of the Code of Ordinances providing for the mooring of vessels in waters of the city, and the impoundment of vessels.
Recently, the Florida legislature adopted Senate Bill 164, and House Bill 481, enacting new regulations regarding anchoring and mooring prohibitions. The proposed amendment to the Code of Ordinances reflects the recent changes adopted by the Florida legislature. The proposed Ordinance expands on the process for impounding vessels, the establishment for impoundment hearings, and provides parameters for the use of City-owned docks and boat ramps, including limitations on the duration of time in which individuals may dock. Additionally, the proposed Ordinance also details specific provisions for live-aboard vessels and commercial vessels, including a maximum period of time in which they may anchor or moor in city waters. Overall, the changes in the proposed Ordinance are intended to bring the City's code up to date with the current statutory provisions, and provide mechanisms for addressing vessels moored or anchored in city waters in violation of City Code.
title: First Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-7 - Amending Chapter 82, Article II - Waterways of the Code of Ordinances

description:
The proposed ordinance amends Chapter 2, Administration, Article III, Boards and Commissions, Division 4, Environmental Advisory Board, Sections 2-118, 2-119, and 2-121 of the City Code to reduce the membership of the Environmental Advisory Board from seven (7) members to five (5) members, revise the Board’s initial appointment structure to reflect the reduced membership, and update the quorum requirement consistent with the revised Board composition.
At the April 26, 2026, Environmental Advisory Board (EAB) meeting, staff discussed the proposed change in membership from seven (7) members to five (5) members. The EAB supported the proposed amendment to reduce the number of Board members to five (5).
Over the past two (2) years, the Board has typically had one to two (1–2) vacancies at any given time, making it difficult to consistently achieve a quorum and conduct meetings. Reducing the Board membership to five (5) members is intended to better align the Board’s structure with current participation levels and improve the likelihood of maintaining a full membership. This adjustment is expected to improve quorum reliability and enhance the Board’s ability to conduct business and provide timely input and recommendations to the City Council.
The ordinance also updates the Environmental Advisory Board’s organizational provisions to align with the revised five-member Board structure, including changes to the Board’s membership composition, appointment schedule, and quorum requirements.
Section 2-118 is revised to establish the Environmental Advisory Board as a five (5)-member board.
Section 2-119 is revised to establish a staggered appointment structure consistent with a five-member Board. The appointments will include two (2) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2027, and three (3) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2030. Pursuant to the City Code, Environmental Advisory Board members serve three (3)-year terms, with all terms expiring in May of the applicable year. Members are eligible for reappointment for any number of consecutive terms.
Section 2-121 is revised to modify the quorum requirement consistent with the reduced Board membership. The amendment changes the quorum requirement from four (4) members to three (3) members, allowing the five-member Board to conduct official business with a majority of appointed members present.
title: First Reading — Ordinance No. 2026-12 - Amendment to Chapter 2, Sections 2-118, 2-119, and 2-121 of the Code of Ordinances for the Environmental Advisory Board Membership, Appointments, Terms, and Rules of Procedure

Attached is the proposed operating budget for the Eastport Business Center CRA tax increment district for FY 2026-2027 (October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027).
The CRA budget is considered prior to the City’s formal budget hearings in September to ensure the CRA Board has sufficient time to review the proposal, provide input, and recommend any necessary adjustments before it is incorporated into the full City budget and adopted by the City Council.
The resolution is also written so that the revenues and expenditures are estimates that can be changed based on the final adopted millage rate and budget. Therefore, the tax increment can be adjusted to the final amount without requiring the CRA Board to reconsider the budget.

The estimated fund balance at the end of FY 2026 is $2,302,345, which may be allocated toward any project identified in the current Eastport CRA Plan, including roadway improvements, development incentives, and drainage and utility upgrades.
An application has been submitted to the Volusia-Flagler TPO for a feasibility study to realign Spruce Creek Road away from the Halifax Canal and widen it to a three-lane section between Dunlawton Avenue and Commonwealth Boulevard. The project also includes intersection improvements to better accommodate heavy truck traffic, enhance driver safety, and increase overall roadway capacity. Funding for the City's portion of the feasibility study, design, and construction will be provided through the CRA’s fund balance.
There are currently three new private development projects (BIK Hydraulics, Sea Tow, and Platinum Powerboats) either underway or proposed within the Eastport area. These projects are expected to attract targeted new businesses and support the expansion of existing businesses.

description:
The City completed an Inflow and Infiltration (I&I) Study in 2015 to identify areas within the sanitary sewer collection system where groundwater and stormwater were entering the system. The study evaluated sewer laterals, gravity mains, and manholes to determine the locations contributing the greatest amount of I&I.
I&I occurs when stormwater and groundwater enter the sanitary sewer system through defects such as cracked pipes, deteriorated manholes, separated joints, or failed service lateral connections. As underground infrastructure ages and shifts over time due to rainfall events, traffic vibrations, and construction activities, these defects can worsen. The City maintains approximately 354 miles of sanitary sewer collection piping and 6,680 manholes, all of which require ongoing inspection and maintenance.
Excessive I&I increases the volume of water conveyed and treated by the wastewater system, resulting in higher treatment and lift station operating costs, increased energy consumption, and a greater potential for sanitary sewer overflows during significant rainfall events. To address these issues, the City has implemented an ongoing repair and rehabilitation (R&R) program focused on reducing I&I within the collection system.
The Hamlet Subdivision has been identified as the next area for sanitary sewer I&I mitigation. The sanitary sewer manholes within the subdivision require rehabilitation. Repairing these structures will help reduce groundwater and stormwater entering the collection system, improving system performance and reducing treatment costs.
On July 18, 2023, City Council approved a Standard Contract for Services with Danus Utilities, Inc. related to ITB #23-07, Sanitary Sewer Manhole Rehabilitation. The City recently executed Renewal No. 2, extending the contract term through July 17, 2027. The agreement includes one remaining renewal option.
The Engineering Department is requesting approval of Task Authorization No. 5 with Danus Utilities, Inc. in an amount not to exceed $255,137 for sanitary sewer manhole rehabilitation within the Hamlet Subdivision.
title: Approval of Task Authorization No. 5 with Danus Utilities, Inc. for the Hamlet Subdivision Sanitary Sewer Manhole Rehabilitation

Staff requests that the City Council waive the formal bidding requirements and approve the attached Professional Services Agreement with Pittman Law Group to provide legislative lobbying services on behalf of the City for the 2026–2028 legislative sessions, with continuation for ensuing legislative sessions unless otherwise terminated in accordance with the agreement.
Pittman Law Group has represented the City for more than 15 years, providing legislative advocacy and strategic guidance before the Florida Legislature and state agencies. Their services include pursuing legislative appropriations and grant funding, monitoring legislation affecting municipalities, coordinating meetings with state legislators and agencies, and advocating for the City's legislative priorities.
The firm's efforts have resulted in significant funding for City infrastructure projects. Since 2022, the City has secured more than $10.5 million in state legislative appropriations, including funding for stormwater and flood mitigation projects identified in the City's Stormwater Master Plan, water quality improvements, utility infrastructure, sewer force main river crossing improvements, water main improvements, and lift station rehabilitation projects. These appropriations have significantly leveraged local funds and advanced priority capital improvements that otherwise would have been difficult to accomplish.
The proposed agreement will allow Pittman Law Group to continue advocating for legislative priorities, state grant opportunities, and other legislative priorities identified by the City Council and City Manager.
Because legislative lobbying services require specialized expertise, established relationships with state legislators and agencies, institutional knowledge of the City's priorities, and continuity of representation, Staff recommends waiving the City's formal bidding requirements. Based on Pittman Law Group's demonstrated success, extensive experience representing the City, and proven ability to secure substantial state funding, Staff believes it is in the City's best interest to continue this professional relationship.

description:
Staff received an application for a License Agreement from the property owners of 220 Charles Street to install a monument sign on the south side of Charles Street within the Charles Street right-of-way, a public right-of-way. The property owner, CBHA Property Holdings, LLC, is requesting the License Agreement to install a monument sign identifying their business (Cool Breeze Heating and Air), along with associated electrical, irrigation, and landscaping improvements within the right-of-way.
The segment of Charles Street right-of-way abutting the 220 Charles Street parcel is approximately 70 feet wide, with the roadway located toward the north side of the right-of-way, leaving approximately 22 feet on the south side between the roadway and the property line for 220 Charles Street. According to the Land Development Code (LDC), a monument sign is required to be set back five (5) feet from the right-of-way line. Therefore, if the proposed sign were installed on the 220 Charles Street parcel pursuant to the setbacks established in the LDC, it would be set back approximately 27 feet from Charles Street, which, according to the property owners, would limit its visibility. The property owners are requesting a License Agreement to allow installation of the sign within the right-of-way so that customers visiting the business can more easily see their sign.
Staff has reviewed the proposed location of the monument sign and determined that installation within the right-of-way would not restrict visibility for vehicles entering or exiting the business, nor would it obstruct sight lines for vehicles traveling east or west on Charles Street.
A building permit for the monument sign has also been submitted to the City for review and complies with the LDC requirements, except for the setback requirement. Issuance of a sign permit is contingent upon the property owner's approval and execution of the License Agreement. The property owners have been advised that, under the License Agreement, installation is limited to the monument sign and associated electrical, irrigation, and landscaping improvements, and that such improvements must not interfere with City utility lines. The property owners are also responsible for maintaining the sign and landscaping.
If the property owners do not comply with the requirements of the License Agreement, the City may take necessary corrective actions at the property owners’ expense. City liability concerns are addressed through an indemnification provision in the License Agreement, and the applicant has provided proof of a $1 million liability insurance policy. If approved, the sign permit will be issued, allowing the sign and landscaping improvements to be installed within the Charles Street right-of-way.
title: Approval of a License Agreement with CBHA Property Holdings, LLC, to install a monument sign within the Charles Street right-of-way at 220 Charles Street

attachments.name: Ord. No. 2026-6 - Port Orange Charter Am re Residency

description:
In a recent election, questions arose regarding the residency requirement for elected officials. The City Charter sets forth the qualifications that must be met to become a candidate and it currently requires that a person seeking to become a candidate be a resident of Port Orange for at least 12 months. While we assume that this means the candidate should be a resident of Port Orange for at least 12 months immediately prior to the election for which the candidate is attempting to qualify and that the residency is continuous in nature, the Charter language is silent as to when the minimum 12 month residency must take place and whether it must be continuous.
After reviewing the relevant case law regarding qualifications for elections along with the current charter language, it became clear that the courts will not assume requirements that are not expressly contained within the charter language. Therefore, in order to be able to enforce what is believed to have been the original intent of the residency provision, an amendment to the Charter is necessary. The proposed addition will specify that the 12 month residence requirement must be both continuous in nature and immediately preceding the qualifying period.
The proposed Charter revision would also add a requirement that proof of residency be submitted by each prospective candidate at the time of qualifying for office along with an affidavit providing residency information and an affirmation that the prospective candidate meets the qualification requirements for the office pursued by the candidate.
Lastly, the Charter is currently silent as to who decides disputes related to qualifications or elections. Therefore, a revision is proposed to make it clear that City Council is the deciding body subject to review by a court of competent jurisdiction. Pursuant to s. 166.031 of the Florida Statutes, City Council must submit the proposed amendment to its Charter to the electors of the City of Port Orange for a vote. The four ballot questions that will show up on the November election are as set forth in Ordinance No. 2026-6. If the amendments are approved by a majority of the voters, the amendments will become effective on January 1, 2027.

attachments.name: Business Impact Estimate - ORD 2026-8 PC-A District LDC Amendment

description:
Note: Summary and Ordinance have been updated from the June 18, 2026 original.
At the June 18 meeting, City Council approved Ordinance No. 2026-08 on first reading, subject to the following revisions:The minimum lot width requirement for detached single-family residential lots within the Community District shall remain 50 feet.
The reference in Figure 17.1 to a density of 16 dwelling units per acre for the 14-acre tract of land has been revised to 8 dwelling units per acre, and Figure 17.2 has been updated to depict the 14-acre tract within the Community District.
The attached Ordinance No. 2026-08 has been revised to incorporate these Council-directed changes.
The original Summary with an updated map is below.
Planning Commission Recommendation (5-28-26): Recommended Approval 5-0
The applicant, Jessica Gow, Esq., on behalf of property owner FL P70 LLC, requests an amendment to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the Land Development Code (LDC) for the Planned Community-Agriculture (PC-A) zoning district. The 1,201-acre PC-A zoning district was established by the City Council in 2002 to support the development of a mixed-use community on the west side of Port Orange. The PC-A zoning district is generally located between Interstate 95 and Tomoka Farms Road, south of the FPL Easement.
Location Map of the PC—A Zoning District
According to the applicant, the proposed text amendments are to update the PC-A zoning district regulations to support continued development of this area in response to existing market demand, by revising the locations of where uses are allowed to be developed within the PC-A while remaining consistent with the current Planned Community-Westside Future Land Use designation, along with minor clean-up revisions, and clarifications to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the LDC.
The PC-A zoning district is required to remain consistent with the underlying Future Land Use (FLU) designation in the Comprehensive Plan for the 1,201-acre PC-A area known as the Planned Community–Westside FLU designation. The Planned Community–Westside FLU designation was adopted in 2002 (formerly known as Planned Community No. 1) along with the PC-A zoning district. The FLU designation establishes the overall development framework for the area, including the following limits and requirements:Maximum overall gross residential density of up to 4 dwelling units per acre (approximately 4,804 total units), with higher densities permitted in designated mixed-use areas, provided the overall density cap of 4 dwelling units per acre is maintained.
The required land use mix, within the PC-A area, shall be within the following range upon buildout:Residential: 35% – 60%
Commercial: 10% – 25%
Industrial: 10% – 25%
Mixed-use town center: 10% – 25%
Conservation/recreation: minimum 10%
Daily Trip cap of 62,600 average daily vehicle trips per day within the PC-A.
Development pattern supporting a central town center, internal connectivity for vehicles and pedestrians, and a transition from higher-intensity uses near Interstate 95 to lower-intensity uses toward the site's outer areas.
Any proposed changes to the PC-A zoning district must remain consistent with the underlying Future Land Use (FLU) designation. The proposed amendment does not change the FLU designation or the limits and development requirements in the Comprehensive Plan for this 1,201-acre property.
According to the applicant, regional development patterns in Volusia County, particularly in the Port Orange and Daytona Beach area, have changed significantly since the PC-A district was originally established about 25 years ago, in 2002. At that time, the PC-A was intended to accommodate a broader mix of employment-based and industrial uses; however, many traditional manufacturing uses have since declined or transitioned toward logistics and distribution-based operations.
Modern industrial and commercial development is increasingly driven by e-commerce growth, demand for same-day and next-day delivery, and direct access to interstate corridors. Over the past several years, the I-4 and I-95 interchange area in Daytona Beach has become the primary location for large-scale warehouse and distribution centers, e-commerce fulfillment facilities, and industrial parks due to its regional connectivity and transportation advantages. In contrast, the PC-A has become less competitive for these uses due to its limited direct interstate access.
As a result, the applicant proposes adjusting the distribution of land uses within the PC-A in response to evolving market conditions while maintaining the overall mixed-use framework. Specifically, the applicant is requesting to reallocate approximately +/- 241 acres from the Workplace District, an employment-focused area intended for commercial and industrial development serving both local and regional markets, to the Community District, a transitional area primarily intended for residential uses, with supporting civic, recreational, and commercial uses.
The proposed amendments to Chapter 17, Section 29 of the Land Development Code (LDC) include: Figures 17.1 and 17.2 are revised to update the PC-A conceptual development plan in the northern area where vacant land remains. The primary change includes approximately +/- 241 acres shifting from the Workplace District to the Community District.
Duplicate and outdated text has been removed
Design standards and permitted uses have been cross-referenced to the appropriate Chapters of the LDC.
Added design flexibility through site plan review for future development in the West Town Center District
Allows development within the Community District to set aside open space areas outside a project's limit, subject to approval of a separate agreement by the City.
Current District Map for the PC-A
Proposed District Map for the PC-A
The applicant is also requesting a reduction in the minimum lot width from 50 feet to 40 feet for single-family lots in the Community District. No changes are proposed to the minimum lot area requirement of 5,000 square feet or to other dimensional standards, including open space, building and driveway setbacks, or depth of on-site parking area. The applicant states that a 40-foot-by-125-foot lot provides additional depth, which can improve layout flexibility compared to a 50-foot-by-100-foot lot. The added depth allows for more usable rear-yard space, greater flexibility in building placement, and the ability to accommodate rear-loaded garages, resulting in a different development pattern and street-facing design along the frontage. Even with a 40-foot-wide lot, typical lot layout, driveway placement, and required setbacks generally still provide sufficient space to accommodate at least one on-street parking space in front of a lot, in addition to the required driveway area.
According to the applicant, the proposed amendment is intended to provide greater flexibility in residential lot design and allow for a wider range of housing types and site layouts in this district. The applicant further indicates that the request is consistent with the intent of the Community District as described in the LDC as a transitional residential area located between the West Town Center District and the surrounding Neighborhood and Workplace Districts to support residential development with strong street frontage interaction, pedestrian connectivity, and integrated circulation networks, including sidewalks, bikeways, alleyways, and on-street parking.
Since 2002, about 610 acres of the 1,201-acre PC-A district have been developed or set aside for conservation. Most development has occurred in the southern part of the district and has been primarily residential. To date, about 452 acres have been developed for residential use, resulting in 2,167 homes (including both single-family and multifamily units).According to the Comprehensive Plan, no more than 721 acres of the PC-A district can be used for residential development, and the maximum gross residential density for the 1,201-acre PC-A district is 4 units per acre. Therefore, about 261 acres of the 1,201 acres could still be developed for residential use. Based on residential development over the last 25 years, developed residential areas average about 4.8 units per acre. If the remaining 261 acres are developed at a similar level, about 1,250 more residential units could be built. In total, the full build-out of the allowed residential development area (721 acres) within the 1,201-acre site would result in approximately 3,400 homes across the 1,201-acre PC-A district. This represents about 1,400 fewer homes than the maximum allowed under the Comprehensive Plan, resulting in an overall gross density of approximately 2.85 homes per acre across the 1,201-acre district.
Overall, the proposed amendment maintains all existing density and intensity (non-residential square footage) limits and does not increase the total average daily vehicle trips per day or the allowable residential or non-residential development beyond what was approved in 2002 with the adoption of the Planned Community–Westside FLU designation.

description: In 2024, the City Council adopted Ordinance No. 2024-22, implementing a negotiated pension enhancement for members of the Fire Pension. The enhancement added up to 300 hours of overtime (OT) each year towards each firefighter’s pensionable compensation. Shortly thereafter, questions arose regarding whether the 300 hours of pensionable OT includes the built-in OT that each firefighter earns as part of the traditional 2,912 hour (24-on / 24-off) shift work – approximately 250 hours each year. IAFF representatives believed that the negotiated enhancement was for an additional 300 hour of OT beyond the mandatory OT worked as part of normal shift work. City staff concurs with that interpretation. Therefore, a clarifying ordinance is needed to accurately describe what the parties believe was the original intent of the pension enhancement.

description:
This is a request for the City Council to establish the tentative maximum fiscal year FY 2026-27 millage rate and schedule the public hearings for the FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget. The maximum millage and budget hearing dates are required public notifications under the Florida Truth in Millage (TRIM) statutes.
The Property Appraiser will use the maximum millage rate voted on during this meeting in the Notice of Proposed Property Taxes and mail it to all property owners in August.
The City Council may reduce the tentative millage rate below the maximum millage rate. However, the City Council cannot increase the tentative millage rate above the maximum millage rate without another public notification to all City property owners. For practical purposes, the rate approved at this meeting will establish the maximum property tax millage rate for the next fiscal year.
The current year's operating millage rate is 4.9750 per $1,000 assessed taxable value; the current year's total taxable value for operating purposes is $6,067,715,038 as certified by the Volusia County Property Appraiser. The current year's rolled-back millage rate is 4.8576 per $1,000 assessed value. If the tentative max millage rate of 5.1500 per $1,000 were assessed, this would be an increase of 6.02% above the rolled back millage rate.
Per Florida Statute Section 200.065, the City Council must hold two public hearings as part of the Truth in Millage (TRIM) process. Staff recommends the public hearing dates and times to be held in the City Council Chambers at City Hall, 1000 City Center Circle, Port Orange, Florida, as follows:
1. Tentative Hearing - Wednesday, September 16, at 5:30 p.m.
2. Final Hearing - Monday, September 28, at 5:30 p.m.

description:
Engineering Staff is requesting approval of Amendment No. 1 to the EJCDC DIS-CMAR525 Agreement with Wharton-Smith for the Force and Water Main River Crossing Construction Project, amending Exhibit B to establish the Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) in an amount not to exceed $11,080,440.00 for the construction of the Force and Water Main River Crossing.
On November 18, 2025, Council approved the award to Wharton-Smith, Inc. for Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR) services for the Force and Water Main River Crossing and for the pre-construction phase – CMAR Pre-construction Services. During the pre-construction phase, Wharton-Smith worked with City Engineering staff and Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. to develop preliminary cost estimates, complete a constructibility review, conduct bidding and procurement of the different work packages, and provided a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) Submittal for the project. The full GMP submittal is attached to this item for further review.
This project will upgrade the potable water and sanitary sewage transmission force mains crossing beneath the Halifax River, providing water and sewer service to Ponce Inlet, Daytona Beach Shores, and Wilbur-by-the-Sea.
The existing 20-inch diameter force main conveys wastewater to serve Ponce Inlet, Daytona Beach Shores, and Port Orange customers located east of Ridgewood Avenue and north of Dunlawton Avenue. Installed in 1986, the pipeline is constructed of ductile iron and is located at a relatively shallow depth beneath the riverbed, leaving it exposed to saltwater conditions that accelerate corrosion and deterioration.
In addition, the existing 24-inch water transmission main, installed in the late 1980s and constructed of ductile iron, is partially located within shallow dredged trenches along the western segment of the crossing and is similarly exposed to saltwater.
This water main is one of only two transmission mains providing potable water and fire protection to Ponce Inlet, Daytona Beach Shores, and unincorporated Wilbur-by-the-Sea, underscoring its critical importance to regional service reliability.
The project is included in the approved Capital Improvement Program (CIP) budget. A total of $2,500,000 for the Force Main portion of the project is being funded through a Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) grant, secured via legislative appropriations with the support of Senator Tom Wright and Representative Chase Tramont.
title: Approval of Amendment No. 1 to the EJCDC DIS-CMAR525 Agreement with Wharton-Smith for the Force and Water Main River Crossing Project amending Exhibit B – Guaranteed Maximum Price Amendment, establishing the Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) for the construction phase of the project

description:
At the October 17, 2023, meeting City Council approved Resolution No. 23-53 authorizing staff to submit an application to the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM) for a Hurricane Nicole Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Grant to demolish and reconstruct one manufactured home.
On March 9, 2026, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) officially awarded funding for the Hurricane Nicole Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) project to demolish and reconstruct one manufactured home located in the Colony in the Wood Subdivision. On April 22, 2026, the City was provided with the Hurricane Nicole Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) Agreement (H1301).
The Hurricane Nicole HMGP Grant Agreement has a total project cost of $210,621.60. Of this amount, $160,473.60, or 75% of the total project cost, is federally funded through HMGP. The remaining $50,148.00, or 25% of the total project cost, represents the required non-federal cost share and will be paid by the participating homeowner prior to the commencement of construction. The homeowners’ 25% cost share is not reimbursable under the HMGP program.
HMGP is a cost-reimbursement grant program with a 75% federal / 25% non-federal cost share requirement. Under HMGP requirements, the homeowner is required to pay the 25% non-federal cost share prior to the commencement of construction, and the City funds the remaining 75% during project implementation. Upon completion of eligible work and submission of the required documentation, FEMA reimburses the City for the eligible 75% federal share of project costs. The homeowner is not eligible to apply directly for HMGP funding; therefore, the City applied for the grant on their behalf and is responsible for administering and overseeing the work.
The reconstruction of this home will significantly reduce the risk of future impacts from future weather events. All demolition and reconstruction activities are voluntary. All activities associated with the demolition and reconstruction will be performed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, and Local Rules and Regulations.
Selection of contractor(s) in compliance with federal procurement requirements is anticipated later this year, and demolition and reconstruction of the home are anticipated to start in early 2027. After bid selection and permitting, the demolition and reconstruction process typically takes 10 months. It is anticipated that the project will be completed in late 2027. According to the HMGP Agreement, the City has until January 31, 2028 to complete this project.
title: Resolution No. 26-30 - Approval of Contract #H1301 for the Hurricane Nicole Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) to Demolish and Reconstruct one home - Port Orange Project CD241

description:
In November 2023, Council approved Resolution No. 23-26 which updated utility rates and the rate structure. These fees were a result of the 2023 Raftelis Financial Consultants, Inc. (Raftelis) rate study regarding the City's water, wastewater, and reclaimed utility rates and other municipal fees. In June 2024, Council approved Resolution No. 24-18 enacting year two of four of the proposed fee adjustments based on the study and framework approved in 2023. In January 2026, Council approved Resolution No. 26-4 enacting year three of four of the proposed fee adjustments. This Resolution enacts year four, the final year, of the proposed fee adjustments. The 5-year Capital Improvements Plan for utilities is based on this multi-year revenue plan as presented to Council.
City fees are actual pass-through costs for water, sewer, and reclaimed utilities. The fee schedule will produce revenues sufficient to meet the projected expenditure requirements of each utility system and maintain a financial position that is both sustainable and consistent with financial performance criteria established by the City. These rates provide a full cost recovery for our utilities. This Resolution incorporates the planned annual increases for our retail and wholesale customers (Daytona Beach Shores and the Town of Ponce Inlet), and development fees as recommended by the Raftelis study through fiscal year 2026-2027, and also eliminates redundant provisions addressing individualized metered mobile home parks.
The recommended annual fee increases will begin on October 1, 2026, for utility customers within Daytona Beach Shores (this schedule is at the Shores' request) and January 1, 2027, for all other utility customers.
The proposed fees will go towards funding the following upcoming notable projects:River Crossing Force Main & Water Main Construction
City-wide Lift Station Rehab
Waste Water Treatment Plant Upgrade
Sewer System Rehabilitation (cleaning, pipelining, manhole lining, etc.)
Emergency Utility Repairs

description:
The Volusia Flagler Family YMCA is requesting a grant from ECHO to fund a portion of the construction of a new ADA playground, a shade structure, and fencing to enclose the playground area. The new ADA playground will include features for all ages and is designed to help children of all abilities learn and grow through play. The playground will be available for siblings, relatives, and friends who visit the Port Orange YMCA during normal operating hours.
The estimated cost for these improvements is $200,000, and the YMCA is requesting a $100,000 grant.
As the property owner, the City is required to sign the application and commit to the 20-year Restrictive Covenants on the property if a grant is awarded. ECHO restrictive covenants are legally binding agreements attached to properties that receive ECHO grant funding. They mandate that funded facilities must provide unrestricted public access, be properly maintained, and be used solely for their approved purpose. The YMCA will be responsible for the matching amount of $100,000 and all costs for keeping the site compliant with the ECHO grant. If the YMCA were to leave the site before the expiration of the 20-year Restrictive Covenants, the City would be required to maintain the site and equipment pursuant to the terms and conditions of the Restrictive Covenants for the remainder of the 20-year term.
