description:
As Hurricane Milton approached the State of Florida, City Council adopted Resolution No. 24-44 declaring a local state of emergency and authorizing the City Manager or his designee to serve as Emergency Management Director. During the local state of emergency, the City Council waived the procedures and formalities required by law and City ordinances and authorized the City Manager to exercise all powers and duties and take all actions deemed appropriate.
The City Manager executed 26 Executive Orders (EO) and requests City Council ratify the actions taken during the local state of emergency. The majority of the EO's (16) were to extend the local state of emergency. The actions taken by the City Manager through executive orders also included providing a temporary increase in spending authority for certain designated employees, providing for the closure of City of Port Orange offices, allowing for telework, temporarily suspending utility shut-offs and late fees for delinquent utility accounts, adopting Volusia County’s curfew, temporary waiver of permit fees for certain repairs and tree removal caused by the Hurricane Milton Storm Event, providing for a procedure for temporary permit fee waiver, providing for certain adjustments for utility charges, and ordering debris removal from private and public rights-of-way.
As part of the recovery efforts from Hurricane Milton, the permit fees for building permits needed to complete repairs to structures damaged by wind, flooding, and falling trees were waived through Executive Order No. 7. The fee waiver for repairs associated with damage due to Hurricane Milton began on October 10, 2024, and will end February 10, 2025. However, due to the processing time for insurance claims and securing contractors to complete the needed repairs, staff is requesting a six (6) month extension through July 28, 2025, for fee waivers for repairs associated with damage due to Hurricane Milton.
title: Resolution No. 25-10 - Ratification of Emergency Powers Taken During Hurricane Milton and Temporarily Extending the Waiver of Certain Permit Fees

description:
The Countryside HOA requests the removal of a 41-inch diameter at breast height (DBH) Live Oak tree. The historic tree is located in a common area owned by the HOA on the south side of Village Trail, east of Country Lane (Figure 1), and was damaged during Hurricane Milton. According to the Land Development Code (LDC), the Environmental Advisory Board is required to recommend a mitigation plan for the removal of a historic tree based on the current tree mitigation resolution adopted by the City Council (Resolution No. 20-46).
In November 2024, the Countryside HOA submitted a tree removal permit to remove a 41-inch diameter at base height (DBH) historic Live Oak tree. The tree has large branches that overhang the Village Trail right-of-way (Figure2). According to the documents submitted with the permit, the HOA is requesting to remove the tree due to damage from Hurricane Milton and the risk posed to vehicles and pedestrians. The City Forester Technician has evaluated the tree and determined that it is a historic Live Oak with a diameter at breast height (DBH) of approximately 41” that has a large wound in the trunk. According to the City Forester Technician, the tree will not be able to heal before rot and decay set in, and the tree will eventually die. Due to the severity of damage to the tree, and the tree has large branches extending that extend over Village Trail, the tree has been determined to be a “high risk” and should be removed.
The LDC defines a Live Oak tree with a 36-inch diameter at breast height (DBH) or greater as a historic tree. According to the LDC, a historic tree that has been damaged by fire, windstorm, lightning, or other acts of God and poses an imminent danger to life or property must still follow the permitting process for tree removal along with mitigating the tree in an amount as established by resolution by the city council. However, if a historic tree is determined to be dead, it still must follow the permitting process for tree removal, but no mitigation is required. According to the City Forester Technician’s report, the historic tree is damaged and deteriorated, but at the time of the evaluation, the tree was not dead; therefore, according to the LDC, the HOA is required to mitigate the removal of the historic tree.
According to the LDC, all historic tree removal permits (alive, damaged, or dead) on land other than single-family and two-family lots, are required to go before the EAB for a recommendation on how the property owner is to mitigate the removal of the historic trees and City Council for final review of the tree removal permit and approval of the mitigation plan. The subject historic tree is located on HOA common area and not a residential lot.
MITIGATION REQUIRED BY THE LDC:
According to the LDC, the EAB may recommend mitigation for removing a damaged historic tree based on the current tree mitigation resolution adopted by the City Council (Resolution 20-46). The EAB may recommend the mitigation for the removal of a damaged historic tree through a combination of planting replacement trees on the subject property and contribution to the city's tree bank, provided that the combination equals or exceeds the required percentage of the total cross-sectional area of the damaged historic tree as established by Resolution 20-46.
The Countryside HOA requests that mitigation for the tree's removal be waived due to it being damaged during Hurricane Milton and that the City Forester Technician's evaluation report concluded the tree will not be able to heal before rot and decay set in, and the tree will eventually die. As stated above, if the historic tree being removed is damaged or deteriorating, it still must follow the permitting process for tree removal, and mitigation is required; however, if a historic tree being removed is determined to be dead, no mitigation is required. Therefore, staff recommends that the mitigation be waived since the damage to this tree will eventually lead to its death, and according to the LDC, no mitigation is required for the removal of a dead historic tree.
Environmental Advisory Board Recommendation:
At their January 27, 2025, meeting, the EAB recommended waiving the mitigation for the removal of the damaged historic tree since the damage to this tree will eventually lead to its death and according to the LDC, no mitigation is required for the removal of a dead historic tree.
The Staff Report is attached for more information.
title: Removal of a Storm Damaged Historic Tree at 940 N Lakewood Terrace in HOA Common Area
Environmental Advisory Board Report - Kristine Cunningham

description:
Anthony Ryan Liszkiewicz, the property owner of 668 Herbert St., is requesting a waiver to keep two Nigerian Dwarf goats on the property. The goats are owned by Mr. Liszkiewicz's sister, Adrienne Liszkiewicz. Animal Control Officer Korey Fox has interviewed the surrounding neighbors who do not feel that the animals will be a nuisance to the community.
City Ordinance 10-12 Limitation of Number of Animals allows residents to have up to fourteen (14) animals that belong to the species of animals listed in the ordinance. Those species are dogs, cats, rabbits, guinea pigs, ferrets, geckos, iguanas, specific birds, gerbils, hamsters, mice, aquarium fish, aquarium amphibians, aquarium reptiles, livestock, and horses, all under specific requirements.
Section 10-12 (g) provides that "any person may apply for a waiver from the limitation on the maximum number of animals and/or species of animals listed in this section by filing a written request with the animal control authority."
The owner, Mr. Liszkiewicz, has requested a waiver based on animal species (Nigerian Dwarf Goat). The animals in question are two Nigerian Dwarf goats, which are 2.5 years old and have reached full size at 24 inches tall and weighing approximately 70lbs. There are no other animals located on the property. The attached survey information for 668 Herbert St., shows the lot size at 16,553 square feet (100 feet X 165 feet/0.38 acre). However, the property owner owns the adjacent lot as well bringing the total to 0.5 acres. An inspection of the home and property was completed on October 4, 2024, by Port Orange Animal Control Officer (ACO) Korey Fox. ACO Fox observed the following as it relates to the factors referenced in the City's Code of Ordinances:
Section 10-12 (i) identifies five (5) factors to be considered when reviewing a waiver request. Those factors are: Conditions of confinement of the animal, including but not limited to sanitation and security:
The animals will live in a 20ft. X 40ft. fenced pen.
The pen is comprised of 5.5ft welded steel panels and gates stay locked to prevent escape.
There will be regular maintenance of the yard to keep the yard clear of feces.
2. The proximity of the animal to adjacent residential property:The lot size is 0.5 acres.
The pen is located on the rear east side of the property furthest from street.
3. Impact of the animal on surrounding property and residents:There appears to be no impact on surrounding properties or residents.
ACO Fox spoke to surrounding neighbors (listed below) who advised that they have no issues with the goats (Miller & Dill) living on the property.662 Herbert St
664 Herbert St
672 Herbert St
105 Judges Ln
4. Nuisance or disturbance to the public caused by the animal; and:The goats (Miller & Dill) are quiet, non-aggressive, and relatively odorless.
They tend to sleep in the sun or eat from the hay feeders.
5. Interest of the public health, safety, and welfare:The goats are both neutered with no upper incisors in the mouth.
The 2.5-year-old goats have reached full size at 24 inches tall and weighing approximately 70lbs which is comparable to a fully grown mid to large breed dog.
Both goats have a microchip implanted
Miller & Dill appear to be happy and healthy.
Staff recommends approving this waiver for the two Nigerian Dwarf goats (Miller & Dill) with the following conditions:
1. The goats are provided necessary care, veterinary shots are kept up to date, and the goats maintain a healthy weight.
2. The fenced enclosure will be maintained to provide adequate confinement.
3. The fenced enclosure will remain secured so that the goats cannot escape.
4. Regular maintenance of the yard will be conducted to keep it free and clear of feces and/or animal waste.5. Any behaviors that may develop in the future that create a nuisance and/or affect the public health, safety and welfare including, but not limited to, any noise issues will be remedied immediately.
If the waiver is granted, the waiver of the species is only for these particular Nigerian Dwarf goats and would not allow for any additional goats without approval.

description:
The Engineering Department is requesting approval of Amendment No. 1 to the AIA Agreement with Wharton-Smith for the Public Utilities Field Operations Facility Construction Project amending Exhibit A - Guaranteed Maximum Price Amendment to establish the Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) in an amount not to exceed $21,887,151.00 for the construction of the Public Utilities Field Operations Facility.
On August 21, 2024, Council approved the award to Wharton-Smith, Inc. for Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR) services for the Public Utilities Operations Facility and for the pre-construction phase – CMAR Preconstruction Services. During the pre-construction phase, Wharton-Smith worked with City Engineering staff and Schenkel Schultz Architects to develop preliminary cost estimates, complete a constructability review, conduct bidding and procurement of the different work packages, and have provided a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) Submittal for the project. The full GMP Submittal is attached to this item for further review.
The current Public Utilities Field Operations facility, built in the 1970s and expanded in the early 1990s, is located on Oak Street, just north of the Public Works yard, but it faces significant space constraints. As a result, some Field Operations staff are based at the wastewater treatment plant, while the heavy equipment needed for their work is stored at other locations across the city. Field Operations plays a vital role in the City’s emergency response team. During potential emergencies, crews must be relocated to the water treatment plant to avoid flooded roads that surround the current facility. The construction of the new Public Utilities facility will bring all of Public Utilities Field Operations and Administrative staff to one centralized location, provide covered storage for equipment which will extend the equipment life, and allow a more efficient operation to better serve the residents of Port Orange.
There are sufficient funds available in the current Fiscal Year CIP Budget to cover expenses prior to the issuance of debt to pay for construction of the facility. Once the debt is secured, Resolution No. 25-02 (which is also on this agenda) allows the City to reimburse itself for incurred project expenditures prior to the issuance of the debt with proceeds from bonds, notes or other obligations to be issued in the future.
If approved, Wharton-Smith plans on breaking ground on the facility in early March 2025 and construction is scheduled for completion in July 2026.

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (12/12/24): Recommended approval 4-0
Lamar Outdoor Advertising is requesting an amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC), allowing the static sign face on existing billboards to be replaced with a digital sign face. If approved, the amendment would allow the City Council the ability to choose to enter into an agreement with a billboard owner to allow the reconstruction of existing billboards along I-95 with a digital sign face in exchange for removing other existing billboards within Port Orange to reduce the number of billboards within Port Orange and improve aesthetics within the City. The proposed amendment would allow a billboard owner to replace a sign face for an existing billboard along I-95 with a digital sign face by removing at least two billboard sign faces.
Under the City's current sign regulations, a billboard is a prohibited sign. Furthermore, structural repairs or reconstruction of existing non-conforming signs is not permitted, requiring them to be removed as they become structurally unsound. The applicant requests this amendment to allow some existing billboards to be reconstructed with a digital sign face in exchange for removing billboards within the City. According to the applicant, Daytona Beach has a similar code to incentivize the removal of billboards within their City in exchange for allowing billboards with a digital sign face on I-95. In addition, cities such as Orlando and St. Petersburg have recently approved ordinances to allow existing billboards along interstates through their City to be reconstructed with a digital sign face in exchange for removing billboards within their City.
There are 13 billboards within Port Orange with the majority of the signs located along I-95. Lamar Outdoor Advertising owns six billboards. If approved on the first reading, a reconstruction agreement between Lamar Outdoor Advertising and the City of Port Orange will be scheduled for Council review with the second reading of this ordinance on February 4, 2025. The proposed reconstruction agreement allows two (2) billboard sign faces along I-95 to be reconstructed with digital sign faces in exchange for removing four (4) billboard sign faces located north of the intersection of Ridgewood Avenue and Nova Road.
Figure 1. General Location of Billboards within Port Orange
The proposed amendment also includes clean-up items to Chapter 15, Section 14, to remove duplicate code requirements that were inadvertently added multiple times when the sign code was updated in 2021 and make the existing digital sign-face requirements in Section 14 consistent with the digital sign-face requirements proposed with this amendment.
The Staff Report is attached for more information.

description:
In October 2025, the City was awarded a $405,130 Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) construction grant for the Riverwalk Park Day Dock project. In September 2026, the City was awarded an additional $292,922 supplemental grant. Together, the two grants total $698,052, representing approximately 43% of the estimated total construction cost of $1,620,520. Staff is requesting Council approval and acceptance of the FIND Grant Agreement in the amount of $292,922 for use toward the construction of the day dock. Matching funds to complete the project are budgeted and available in Project #PK242.
The design of the day dock is complete, and all required permits have been obtained. The City will advertise the project for construction bids later this year. Construction is expected to begin in early 2027, with completion expected in late 2027.
The project includes a floating day dock oriented perpendicular to the shoreline, providing mooring for up to ten (10) vessels, with the ability to expand in the future as demand increases. The dock is also designed to accommodate a future water taxi stop. The design plans include a dredging profile to establish a navigable access channel between the day dock and the adjacent deep-water channel leading to the Intracoastal Waterway (ICW), as well as channel markers connecting the dock to the existing marked channel. The day dock is intended for daytime use only; however, electrical conduit to accommodate future lighting if nighttime use is desired will be installed.

description:
The Port Orange Police Department (POPD) has demonstrated continued success in implementing FDOT-funded motorcycle safety initiatives and has been awarded this funding for the second consecutive year. Through the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Motorcycle Safety and Awareness High Visibility Enforcement Campaign, POPD conducted 153 motorcycle safety enforcement operations, made 918 public contacts, and completed five motorcycle safety outreach and educational activities. Building upon these successful outcomes, FDOT increased the City's FY2027 award from $40,000 in FY2026 to $50,000 in FY2027, reflecting continued confidence in the City's ability to effectively promote motorcycle safety through education, awareness, and enforcement efforts.
The POPD seeks to utilize $50,000 in FY2027 awarded funding to engage in a proactive approach to reduce the number of motorcycle-related serious injuries/fatality crashes within the City.
POPD staff utilized data from the FY2026 Highway Safety Matrix- Ranking of Florida counties (population 200,001 and above) which illustrates that motorcycle safety was a major contributor to traffic crashes and fatalities in Volusia County, ranking 4 out of 26 counties of a similar size in the State of Florida. Additionally, out of 105 cities with a population of 15,000-74,999, the City ranked 11th highest for motorcyclist-related crashes and fatalities.
The campaign will focus on conducting motorcyclist-focused enforcement operations throughout the funding period to address motorcyclists for safety issues and violations of state statutes. Officers will also conduct traffic stops on other motor vehicle drivers for committing violations deemed dangerous to motorcyclists. Officers will focus their attention on the roadways with the highest rate of motorcycle-related crashes.
Additionally, high visibility enforcement operations will be increased during any bike events occurring in the area.
Lastly, the POPD staff will utilize a combination of social media communication, and electronic message boards along roadways to display motorcycle-related safety messages.
The funds will be used to provide additional high-visibility patrols that focus on motorcycle safety and awareness through education and enforcement. Personnel assigned to this initiative will be paid overtime through this funding and will not affect minimum patrol staffing levels. Staff participating in this program will receive the required training.
The grant will be concluded prior to the end of the 2027 fiscal year, and there are no match requirements.
title: Resolution No. 26-54- Approval of a Subgrant Agreement with the Florida Department of Transportation accepting a grant in the amount of $50,000 for a Motorcycle Safety and Awareness High Visibility Enforcement Campaign

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (October 29, 2026): Recommended Approval 5-0
The applicant is requesting the Fifth Amendment to the Journey’s End Planned Commercial Development (PCD) Master Development Agreement (MDA) and Conceptual Development Plan (CDP) to facilitate development of the property at 5800 Journey’s End Way, located between the existing Hanwoo Korean BBQ restaurant and the Country Inn & Suites Hotel.
According to the applicant, the proposed amendment would allow the subject property to be developed as a hotel and establish a conceptual framework for the development, including the hotel’s location, building height, and access. If approved, the applicant proposes to construct a Home2 Suites by Hilton hotel with approximately 95 guest rooms. The applicant describes Home2 Suites by Hilton as an all-suite hotel brand that primarily serves extended-stay guests while also accommodating shorter stays. According to the applicant, the hotel would most likely serve business travelers, families, leisure travelers, and individuals seeking temporary accommodations for work, relocation, or other needs.
Location Map of the Subject Property — 5800 Journey’s End Way
The subject property is a 1.36-acre vacant parcel within the Journey’s End PCD, identified as Lot 2. The City Council originally approved the Journey's End PCD in 2000 and established three commercial lots, including the subject property. In 2008, the City Council approved the First Amendment to the Journey’s End PCD, adding two additional commercial lots and bringing the total number of commercial lots within the PCD to five.
Four of the five commercial lots within the Journey’s End PCD have been developed. The subject property is the only remaining undeveloped commercial lot, surrounded by existing commercial and hospitality development to the north and south and abutting I-95 to the west. To the east, the subject property abuts properties outside the PCD zoned Community Commercial (CC) or Agriculture (A). Only a small portion, approximately 43 feet of the 243-foot rear property line, abuts the Agriculture-zoned property, which is developed with a residential use.
If the amendment is approved, the applicant proposes to develop the subject property as a Home2 Suites by Hilton with approximately 95 rooms. The applicant is requesting approval of the following amendments to the Journey’s End PCD Master Development Agreement (MDA):Add “hotel” as a permitted use for Lot 2. The existing PCD allows a variety of commercial uses on Lot 2, including restaurants, offices, retail, and health and fitness clubs; however, a hotel is not currently permitted on this lot. Hotels are already permitted on two other commercial lots within the PCD. The amendment would add hotels to the existing list of permitted commercial uses for Lot 2.
Increase the allowable building height for Lot 2 from 45 feet to 55 feet. The applicant is requesting additional height to accommodate the proposed hotel. The proposed 55-foot maximum would remain below the 60-foot maximum already permitted on two other properties within the Journey’s End PCD, including the Country Inn & Suites hotel and Extra Space Storage facility, and the 65-foot maximum allowed in the City’s Interchange Commercial Development (ICD) zoning district. The Conceptual Development Plan shows the hotel building approximately 78 feet from the eastern property line, compared with the minimum required 25-foot setback, providing additional separation from the adjacent property to the east. The existing Master Development Agreement also requires a 10-foot landscape buffer and a 6-foot fence along the eastern property line.
Revise the Conceptual Development Plan to establish a conceptual site layout for the proposed hotel, including the building footprint, parking, access, and landscape buffers. It would also provide for minor modifications to the adjacent Country Inn & Suites property, including relocating the dumpster and restriping the rear parking lot, to accommodate a cross-access connection between the two properties.
Conceptual Development Plan

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (October 29, 2026): Recommended Approval 5-0
At the October 6, 2026 meeting, City Council approved Resolution No. 26-51, stating its intent to adopt a 12-month moratorium on data centers of any size proposed on private property. The next step is for the City Council to consider an ordinance formally establishing the moratorium.
The moratorium would give staff time to evaluate the potential impacts of data centers and other large-load utility users, assess the adequacy of existing regulations, and develop potential amendments to the City’s Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code (LDC).
Data center technology is evolving rapidly, and these facilities can place significant demands on land, water, electricity, and other resources. These demands present challenges for local governments seeking to address potential impacts on surrounding properties, public infrastructure, and natural resources.
In 2026, the Florida Legislature enacted Senate Bill 484 (SB 484), Chapter 2026-65, Laws of Florida, which became effective July 1, 2026. The legislation expressly preserves local governments’ authority to regulate large-load customers through comprehensive planning and land development regulations. This authority allows the City to evaluate whether its Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code adequately address data centers and other large-load utility users and whether additional or revised regulations are needed to address land use compatibility, infrastructure capacity, environmental impacts, and public facilities and services.
Potential regulations could address definitions, appropriate zoning districts, whether data centers should be permitted uses or subject to Conditional Use review, and standards for setbacks, separation from residential uses, noise, building scale, water resources, electrical infrastructure, landscaping and buffering, backup generators, traffic, emergency services, and other potential impacts. The review may also identify a need for different standards based on facility size, operational characteristics, and resource demands.
Because these regulations involve land use, any necessary changes to the City’s Comprehensive Plan and LDC must follow the applicable public hearing and adoption procedures. Neither the City’s current Comprehensive Plan nor its LDC specifically addresses data centers, making it important to evaluate whether additional policies and development standards are needed.
During the moratorium, the Community Development Department will work with the City Attorney’s Office to evaluate regulatory options and develop reasonable, legally enforceable regulations for City Council consideration. Any proposed Comprehensive Plan or LDC amendments will be reviewed by the Planning Commission and City Council and will follow applicable public hearing and adoption procedures.
title: First Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-16 - Moratorium - Data Centers (Case No. DCAM-26-0006)

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (October 29, 2026): Recommended Approval 5-0
Compliance with New State Law (HB 399)
This proposed amendment to the Land Development Code (LDC) updates the City’s regulations to comply with House Bill 399 (HB 399), signed by the Governor on March 27, 2026, and effective January 1, 2027. The law addresses homes built entirely or partially at a factory or another location and then transported to a residential property for installation. These homes include qualifying manufactured homes and are referred to in HB 399 and this amendment as “off-site-constructed residential dwellings.”
Currently, Port Orange permits manufactured homes only on properties zoned Mobile Home Residential (RMH) or within a Planned Unit Development (PUD) that specifically allows manufactured homes as a permitted use. Under HB 399, the City must allow qualifying off-site-constructed residential dwellings (manufactured homes) in the same zoning districts where single-family detached homes are permitted. The City may not regulate these dwellings more restrictively than comparable site-built homes. The proposed amendments include the following:
Chapter 2 – Definitions: Revise the definition of “dwelling” to distinguish between on-site and off-site construction; add a definition for “off-site-constructed residential dwelling”; and update related definitions for manufactured buildings, manufactured homes, mobile homes, park trailers, recreational vehicles, and their associated parks and subdivisions to align with state law.
Chapters 17 and 18 – Zoning Districts and Permitted Uses: Add off-site-constructed residential dwellings as a permitted use, or as a permitted use subject to special development requirements, in applicable zoning districts where single-family detached dwellings are allowed. These districts include:Agricultural Preservation (AP)

description:
PLANNING COMMISSION ACTION (October 29, 2026): Recommended Approval 5-0
The proposed amendment to Chapter 9 of the LDC will align the City’s residential dock setback waiver provisions with the residential dock setback waiver provisions established by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP). In 2025, the LDC was amended to update residential dock and boathouse requirements, including provisions that allow adjacent single-family parcels to share a dock through a setback waiver and allow docks on lots with less than 65 feet of shoreline to be centered between property lines. The proposed amendment also adds an FDEP waiver provision allowing a portion of a dock or other authorized structure to extend into a required setback when necessary to avoid or minimize impacts to natural resources, such as seagrass beds, mangroves, and other sensitive aquatic habitats. These requests require thorough review and approval by FDEP, including an evaluation of the proposed dock location and its potential impacts on natural resources, as well as written consent from the affected adjacent upland riparian owner. The amendment clarifies that once FDEP reviews and approves a setback waiver, the City will allow the reduced setback in accordance with FDEP’s approval, maintaining consistency between the LDC and FDEP requirements.

description:
Each year, the City amends its Comprehensive Plan Capital Improvements Element (CIE) to reflect projects included in the City’s current Capital Improvements Program (CIP). The City has historically completed this annual update around this time of year, after adopting the City’s budget and CIP. The CIE identifies capital improvements needed to maintain adopted level of service (LOS) standards for public facilities, including water, sewer, stormwater, solid waste, roads, parks, and schools.
The City Council adopted the FY 2026–2031 CIP as part of the FY 2027 Operating and Capital Budgets on September 28, 2026, by Resolution No. 26-50. The proposed CIE amendments incorporate applicable projects from the adopted FY 2027–2031 CIP into the Comprehensive Plan. The City Council has already approved these projects by adopting the FY 2026–2031 CIP; the amendments update the CIE to reflect those previously approved projects.
State law requires local governments to update their CIE annually to show that they have funded, or plan to fund, the public facility improvements needed to support their population. The proposed amendments in Exhibit A must be in underline/strikethrough format. For each table or text that is to be updated from the prior year CIP (FY26 – FY30) to the current year CIP (FY27 – FY31), the deleted prior year text is shown in strikethrough (strikethrough) format, and the added current year text is underlined (underlined). Text that is not struck through or underlined remains as existing text in the FY27-31 CIE.
The Staff Report is attached for more information.

description:
The proposed ordinance amends Chapter 50, Parks and Recreation, Article III, Parks and Recreation Board, Sections 50-58, 50-59, and 50-61 of the City Code to reduce the membership of the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board from seven (7) members to five (5) members, revise the Board’s initial appointment structure to reflect the reduced membership, and update the quorum requirement consistent with the revised Board composition.
The Parks and Recreation Advisory Board supports the proposed amendment to reduce the number of Board members to five (5).
In recent years, the Board has typically had one to two (1–2) vacancies at any given time, making it difficult to consistently achieve a quorum and conduct meetings. Reducing the Board membership to five (5) members is intended to better align the Board’s structure with current participation levels and improve the likelihood of maintaining a full membership. This adjustment is expected to improve quorum reliability and enhance the Board’s ability to conduct business and provide timely input and recommendations to the City Council.
The ordinance also updates the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board’s organizational provisions to align with the revised five-member Board structure, including changes to the Board’s membership composition, appointment schedule, and quorum requirements.
Section 50-58 is revised to establish the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board as a five (5)-member board.
Section 50-59 is revised to establish a staggered appointment structure consistent with a five-member Board. The appointments will include two (2) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2027, and three (3) members appointed for terms expiring May 7, 2030. Pursuant to the City Code, Parks and Recreation Advisory Board members serve three (3)-year terms, with all terms expiring in May of the applicable year. Members are eligible for reappointment for any number of consecutive terms.
Section 50-61 is revised to modify the quorum requirement consistent with the reduced Board membership. The amendment changes the quorum requirement from four (4) members to three (3) members, allowing the five-member Board to conduct official business with a majority of appointed members present.
title: First Reading - Ordinance No. 2026- 20 - Amendment to Chapter 50, Article III, Sections 50-58, 50-59, and 50-61 of the Code of Ordinances for the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board Membership, Appointments, Terms, and Rules of Procedure

description:
The City's purchasing process is governed by Chapter 2, Article VI, Division 2, of the Code of Ordinances and further detailed in the Administrative Purchasing Policy. Staff has been methodically evaluating and improving procurement practices to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and accountability while ensuring fair and competitive pricing and maximizing opportunities for vendors to provide goods and services to the City.
As part of these improvements, the City has transitioned its financial and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system to Tyler Technologies and is now implementing OpenGov, an online procurement platform designed to automate and streamline purchasing activities. OpenGov will modernize the solicitation and bid submission process, improve vendor access and participation, strengthen internal controls, and provide greater efficiency throughout the procurement process.
Staff has also reviewed the City's existing purchasing ordinances and policies and identified several areas where amendments are needed to support these improvements. This proposed ordinance represents the first phase of those changes and addresses bidding procedures, emergency purchases, the City Manager's purchasing authority, contract modifications, and bid protests.
The proposed amendments increase the City Manager's purchasing authority from $25,000, established over a decade ago, to $50,000. This increase applies to securing goods and services and for certain routine, exempt, single-response, and emergency purchases, and contract change orders. Finance Staff reviewed purchasing authority thresholds established by other Florida municipalities, along with guidance from the Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) and the National Institute of Governmental Purchasing (NIGP). The proposed $50,000 threshold is consistent with several area municipalities, including New Smyrna Beach, Orange City, DeBary, and DeLand, and remains conservative compared to other municipalities, such as Ormond Beach and Deltona, which allow City Manager approval up to $75,000 and up to $100,000 in Daytona Beach Shores. The adjustment also better reflects the increased cost of goods and services in recent years.
Another amendment will modernize bidding requirements to accommodate electronic solicitations and submissions through OpenGov. The current code requires paper submittals, and the revision will allow a fully electronic process.
The amendments also establish a 1% bid protest bond requirement to help ensure protests are submitted in good faith. The bond would be refunded if the protest is upheld or all bids are rejected.
Collectively, these changes are intended to reduce unnecessary administrative delays and improve procurement efficiency while maintaining appropriate financial controls and City Council oversight of higher-value expenditures.
Importantly, the amendments do not eliminate competitive procurement requirements or existing audit requirements. City Council approval will continue to be required for purchases and contracts exceeding $50,000, except as otherwise provided in the Code. All purchases remain subject to available budget appropriations, applicable internal controls, and Federal and State requirements.
This ordinance represents the first phase of a broader effort to modernize and improve the City's purchasing processes. Additional amendments and procedural updates are anticipated in the near future to further strengthen and streamline procurement operations. Once all proposed changes have been completed, the City's Purchasing Manual will be comprehensively updated to incorporate the revised requirements and procedures.
In summary, the proposed amendments modernize the City's purchasing procedures, align purchasing authority more closely with current municipal practices, and establish the framework necessary to implement a more transparent and efficient online procurement system while maintaining accountability and appropriate City Council oversight.

description:
The South Oak Townhouses Homeowners Association (SOTHA), the property owner, requests removal of a historic Live Oak tree with a 39-inch diameter at breast height (DBH) because it is close to a townhouse at 3656 Jackson Street. The tree is located within the development’s common area, directly behind the rear patio of Unit C10, between the townhouse and Herbert Street (Figure 1). SOTHA owns and maintains the common area. According to the arborist report SOTHA obtained and a site visit, the tree is approximately one foot from the townhouse structure. In September 2026, SOTHA submitted a tree removal permit to remove the historic Live Oak tree, which measures 39 inches in DBH. Ray Jarrett, Biologist/Arborist, evaluated the tree and determined that it is a historic Live Oak measuring approximately 39 inches DBH and 70 feet tall (Exhibit 1), with no visible signs of disease.
Figure 1. Map showing the location of the historic tree
According to the Volusia County Property Appraiser, the townhouse development was constructed in 1984. Based on the available information, the townhouse, specifically Unit C10, appears to have been built adjacent to the existing Live Oak tree, which has grown over time and is now impacting the structure. During development, the developer retained several existing trees and built the townhouses and parking areas around them. Although these trees have continued to grow, the development's existing tree cover remains substantial. Removal of the subject tree would therefore still leave a substantial number of trees within the development.
Although each townhouse unit functions as a separate dwelling, the units are part of an attached residential development, and the subject tree is located within the common area owned by SOTHA rather than on an individually owned townhouse lot. The Land Development Code (LDC) defines a multifamily dwelling as “A building containing three or more dwelling units which would include the following types: Single-family attached; Apartments, low and mid-rise; and Townhouses.” Accordingly, the townhouse development is classified as multifamily rather than single-family residential.
This request is similar to the historic Live Oak tree removal request for the townhome at 164 Sweetgum Lane, which the Environmental Advisory Board (EAB) considered and City Council approved in early 2026. Both requests involve a historic Live Oak adjacent to a townhouse in an attached residential development, with concerns about the tree’s impact on the structure.
According to the arborist’s report, the tree is located directly behind the townhouse at 3656 Jackson Street, with the main trunk approximately one foot from the rear patio wall (Figure 2). The report indicates that the tree’s root system is contributing to the impacts to the structure. SOTHA reports that the porch is pulling away from the townhouse and the walkway is being lifted (see Figure 3). The arborist identifies potential impacts to the patio wall, walkway, and areas where the porch connects to the townhouse, and notes that these conditions could continue or worsen as the tree grows. According to SOTHA and the owner of Unit C10, they have not undertaken repairs because they believe the impact may continue while the tree remains in place. Following removal, SOTHA and the owner of Unit C10 intend to assess the condition of the patio, walkway, and dwelling and complete any necessary repairs.
Figure 2. Pictures of the subject tree proximity to Unit C10
Figure 3. Picture of damaged patio and walkway
According to the arborist report, root pruning is not a suitable option because removing the roots needed to address the structural impacts could weaken the tree and increase the potential for failure. The tree also leans toward Herbert Street, creating an additional concern that, if it fails, it could fall toward the roadway, potentially obstructing traffic, damaging the townhouse or City infrastructure, and bringing down power lines (see Figure 4).
Figure 4. Picture of subject tree leaning over Herbert Street
Although the tree shows no signs of disease, the SOTHA states that the request aims to address existing impacts and prevent further damage to the townhouse as the tree and its root system continue to grow. The reported separation of the porch from the townhouse and lifting of the walkway indicate that impacts are already occurring. According to the SOTHA, removal is being requested as a preventive measure to avoid more extensive structural damage and reduce the potential risks associated with the tree’s proximity to the townhouse and Herbert Street.
The LDC defines a Live Oak tree with a 36-inch diameter at breast height (DBH) or greater as a historic tree. According to the LDC, all historic tree removal permits on land other than single-family and two-family lots must go before the EAB for a recommendation on appropriate mitigation for removing the historic tree, if the City Council ultimately approves the request. The City Council provides final review and approval of the historic tree removal permit and the associated mitigation plan.
Mitigation Required by the LDC:
According to the LDC, the EAB may recommend mitigation for removing a historic tree, as provided by City staff, based upon the current tree mitigation resolution adopted by the City Council (Exhibit 2 - Resolution No. 20-46). The EAB may allow the mitigation for the removal of a historic tree through a combination of planting replacement trees on the subject property and contribution to the City's tree bank, provided that the combination equals or exceeds the required percentage of the total cross-sectional area of the historic tree as established by Resolution No. 20-46. Exhibit A of the resolution is used in this case since the arborist report states the historic tree is healthy.
Mitigation Options:
39” Live Oak Tree
a. Payment of $4,838.09 into the tree bank (39-inch DBH @ 15% cross-sectional area = 179.19 x $27.00); or
b. Plant 11 trees on the subject property. The replacement trees shall be 4.5” caliper measured 12” above ground and 14’ tall; or
c. A combination of payment into the tree bank and replacement trees.
SOTHA requests that the mitigation be waived because of the safety concerns the tree poses to the adjacent townhome. The HOA has stated that if the tree were located on a detached single-family home lot, the Florida Statute exemption in Section 163.04 F.S. would apply and allow removal without a permit or mitigation. The Arborist report indicates the tree presents a moderate risk to the adjacent townhome and meets the statutory criteria for removal. However, because the property is classified as multi-family, this exemption does not apply, and tree removal must comply with the City’s Land Development Code requirements. Based on the arborist’s assessment, the tree’s potential for failure and high impact on the residence demonstrates that removal is the only practical solution to protect the property.
EAB Recommendation (10-26-26):
The Environmental Advisory Board (EAB) recommended approval of the mitigation payment option at $4,838.09, calculated based on the removal of a 39-inch DBH historic tree located on a multifamily parcel.
After the vote, the EAB supported the property owner’s request that the City Council waive the mitigation fee, citing the damage the tree caused and the anticipated cost for removal if the request is approved.
The Staff Report, which includes the Arborist Report, is attached for more information.
title: Approval to Remove a Historic Live Oak Tree at 3656 Jackson Street

description:
In 2024, Vice Mayor Tracy Grubbs requested that Council discuss implementing a surcharge on monthly utility bills for customers who elect to receive a paper statement by mail to help offset the associated costs. The topic was revisited by Council in October 2026, at which time Staff was directed to provide additional information for Council's consideration and direction.
Currently, approximately 62% (18,400) of the City's 29,400 utility customers receive their monthly utility bills as printed statements delivered through the U.S. Postal Service. The 2021 water and sewer rate study estimated the annual cost of preparing and mailing paper utility bills at approximately $185,000. This expense was incorporated into the overall cost of providing water and sewer services and included in the rates established at that time. In 2021, approximately 21,000 paper statements were mailed each month. Since then, the number of customers receiving paper statements has decreased to approximately 18,400; however, increased mailing and related costs have resulted in the City's current budgeted expense exceeding $200,000 annually. These costs include envelopes, paper, bulk postage, occasional inserts, and other associated mailing expenses. Based on the City's current contract amount, the estimated cost to prepare and mail each statement is approximately $1.00.
Under the concept discussed at previous Council meetings, customers who elect to receive a paper utility bill would be assessed a surcharge with each billing cycle. The surcharge amount would be determined by Council, with $1.00 used in the example below to illustrate full cost recovery of the approximately $220,000 contract. Customers who choose electronic delivery would not be assessed the surcharge.
Customers can change their delivery preferences online, which automatically updates the City's utility billing system. However, the City's current billing software does not have an automated process to apply the surcharge. As a result, Staff would need to review each billing cycle and manually apply the surcharge to accounts receiving a printed statement.
The fiscal impact will depend on the number of customers who continue to receive paper statements. If all 18,400 current paper-bill customers continue to receive printed statements, a $1 monthly surcharge would generate approximately $220,800 in annual revenue. Actual revenue will vary as customers transition to electronic delivery.
